en: The transliteration emulates the conventions of the Nāgarī script;
therefore, many word boundaries are not marked by spaces.
*Sphuṭārthā Śrīghanācārasaṃgrahaṭīkā* (The Clear Meaning Commentary on the Compendium of the Glorious Ghanācāra).
Homage to the Buddha.

With palms joined in reverence, I bow down many times to all the Buddhas— those who have abandoned every trace of defilement without exception, who have conquered their enemies, who have gone to the further shore of the ocean of the knowable, who are compassionate, and who are accompanied by the assembly of true disciples of the sublime Dharma.

I bow to Mañjuśrī, the auspicious wish-fulfilling tree, whose roots of excellent conduct are nourished by the sprinkling of the water of generosity; whose beauty arises from the sprouts of loving-kindness and compassion; which bears the fruit of the factors of enlightenment and the path; and which is frequented by the bees that are the Victors.
For the sake of the recollection of this *Ācārasaṃgraha*, this *Viniścaya* is composed as a summary of the extensive sūtras for those of dull intellect.

In this regard, for the most part, virtuous people, having worshipped their guru and chosen deity, engage in an activity for the sake of generating merit, as well as for the sake of pacifying obstacles and for the sake of auspiciousness.
And I too, considering this to be the conduct of the virtuous, have set out to perform a salutation to my own deity at the commencement of the *Śrīghana-cārasaṃgraha*; showing this, he says:
"Having abandoned all afflictions," and so forth.

In that regard, there are three kinds of affliction (*saṃkleśa*): the affliction of defilements (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), the affliction of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*), and the affliction of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*).
They are called "defilements" (*kleśa*) because they afflict the body, speech, and mind.
And those [afflictions], such as attachment and so forth, number one hundred and eight:
namely, ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).
Affliction itself is the defilement; thus, it is called "affliction-defilement" because its intrinsic nature is affliction and because it is the cause of affliction-defilement.
If one asks, "Of what is it the cause of affliction-defilement? we reply: "It is the cause of karma-defilement.
For those whose hearts are consumed by the fire of affliction...
They seek to plunge into what appears in the form of the water of a mirage, though it is [merely] wholesome.
Action is threefold: bodily, vocal, and mental.
Bodily action is also threefold: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
In this same way, the vocal and mental [actions] should be understood in detail.
Action itself is the defilement; it is "defilement of action" because it produces defilement and because it is the cause of defilement.
One should understand that its quality of producing defilement arises from being generated by the defilement of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because it is the cause of birth and affliction (*janmakleśa*), it is the cause of defilement (*saṃkleśahetu*).
Birth (*janma*), arising (*utpatti*), and manifestation (*prādurbhāva*) are synonymous.
Birth itself is defilement; thus, it is "defilement of birth" (*janmasaṃkleśa*). This is because it is the fruit of the defilement of birth and because it is itself the cause of defilement.
Since birth occurs for those possessed of passion due to the defilement of karma— given that the birth of one free from passion is not observed— therefore,

because it is the fruit of the defilements of affliction and karma, and because it is the cause of the defilement of afflictions, it is called the "defilement of birth. For this very reason, its explanation is neither too brief nor too extensive, just like that of the Three Jewels.
Now, the compound is a *bahuvrīhi* consisting of three words:

he is one by whom the Blessed Buddha has abandoned (*prahīṇa*), relinquished (*parityakta*), removed (*apanīta*), or set aside (*tiraskṛta*) all (*aśeṣa*) or entire (*nikhila*) afflictions (*saṃkleśa*)—including their latent predispositions (*vāsanā*)—which are known as afflictions, karma, and birth;
thus he is "one who has abandoned all afflictions without remainder."
By this, he demonstrates the perfection of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃpad*) of the Buddha, the Blessed One.
But should it not simply be said that "the afflictions have been abandoned"?
What is the purpose of including the term "without remainder" (*aśeṣa*)?
This is not so;
if one were to say merely that he has abandoned the afflictions, then it would follow that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas would also be included.
They too have abandoned the afflictions because of the absolute absence of afflicted ignorance;
however, they have not abandoned all afflictions because of the absolute absence of non-afflicted ignorance.
Nevertheless, for these Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas, regarding the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and so forth—

Regarding the dharmas of the Tathāgata, which extend across many world-systems and are distinguished by the divisions of past and future times, there is indeed no undefiled ignorance. Furthermore, Sāriputra, do you perceive the aggregate of morality, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of the Tathāgata?
When questioned, he replied, "No, Venerable Sir," because according to the Sūtra, the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana did not know the birthplace of his own mother,
and because the noble Śāriputra rejected a man seeking ordination, and because [the Buddha] did not know the specific karma that produces the eye of a peacock's tail and so forth;
therefore, let there be no inclusion of them.

"Jñeya" (the knowable), "boddhavya" (that which is to be understood), and "parijñātavya" (that which is to be fully known) are synonymous. A "nidhi" is a receptacle or support, so called because entities are deposited (*ni-dhīyante*) or established within it.
An "ambhonidhi" is a storehouse of waters—that is, of water.
For in the world, the term "ocean" (ambhonidhi) is well-known as referring to an external object;
however, here, by virtue of its similarity to that, just as the great ocean is called an "ocean" because it is deep and exceedingly difficult to cross,
so too is the object of knowledge (jñeya) an "ocean," because it is difficult to fully comprehend and because it is unfathomable due to being entirely unknowable.

The "ocean of the knowable" (*jñeyāmbhonidhi*) refers to the ocean that is the knowable itself. One who goes to the further shore of this ocean of the knowable is called "one who has gone to the further shore of the ocean of the knowable" (*jñeyāmbhonidhipāraga*), just as one is said to have gone from this shore to the other shore.
By this [epithet], he also demonstrates the perfection of knowledge (*jñānasaṃpad*) of the One Possessing the Ten Powers (*daśabala*).

He has abandoned all afflictions without exception and has reached the further shore of the ocean of the knowable; thus, he is "one who has abandoned all afflictions without exception and has reached the further shore of the ocean of the knowable.

Therefore, having bowed to him—who has abandoned all afflictions without exception and reached the further shore of the ocean of the knowable—to that distinguished Buddha, the Blessed One, with body, speech, and mind; this is the ellipsis.
The suffix *ktvā* is prescribed for two actions performed by the same agent when one occurs prior to the other; thus, [the author says] "having prostrated" (*praṇamya*).
For example, as in "having bathed, he eats" (*snātvā bhuṅkte*).
Therefore, it is asked: "To whom having prostrated will you do what? He replies: "The conduct of the novices (*śrāmaṇera*) will be compiled."
In this context, they are called *śrāmaṇeras* because they go toward or enter the lofty city of Nirvāṇa, which is the goal of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇya*).
Alternatively, they are called *śrāmaṇeras* because they go toward or enter the stainless path that constitutes the ascetic life.
Some say they are the servants (*erā*) of those who lead the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇānām*).
What [is the purpose] of these? Conduct (*ācāra*) will be compiled. Conduct is the act of practicing; its meaning is the avoidance of the unwholesome and the cultivation of the wholesome.
But if this is so, does it not follow that the text itself cannot be considered conduct, because it is of the nature of a composition (*kriyā*)?
This is not a fault.
For even a text that sets forth conduct is called "conduct" by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), as in the cases of the *Jātakamālā* and the *Kaṃsavadha*.
Since one practices [conduct] therein, the *Śrīghana-ācārasaṃgraha* itself is designated by the word "conduct."
It is called "compendium" (saṃgraha) because it will be compiled;
that is to say, it will be composed or undertaken. The words "by me" are the ellipsis to be supplied at the end of the sentence.
Otherwise, he would have given the instruction using the first person alone,
intending to include his own conduct as well.
In brief, in this verse, the perfection of abandonment and the perfection of knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, [are set forth].

The state of being the teacher of the three worlds and the cause of teaching without error are elucidated by the phrases "one who has abandoned all afflictions" and "one who has reached the further shore of the ocean of the knowable.
For the state of having abandoned all afflictions does not exceed the perfection of abandonment.
And having reached the further shore of the ocean of the knowable, he possesses the perfection of knowledge;
one who is devoted to the knowledge consisting of the perfection of abandonment and the perfection of knowledge becomes the teacher of the three worlds, a teacher of things as they truly are.
The perfection of abandonment and knowledge, the state of being the sole teacher in the three worlds,
and the cause of the authentic teaching have been set forth in sequence by means of this verse.
Thus is the summary verse. // 1 //

"It shall be a refuge," and so forth. [Objection: But since it was stated immediately prior that "conduct (ācāra) will be included," conduct ought to have been included; why then is taking refuge and so on mentioned?
[Response: Even though this was the subject at hand immediately following the section on the novices (śrāmaṇera), such that the conduct of the novices would have been included—
Furthermore, it is specifically those novice monks who are embraced by the ten precepts (*daśa-śikṣā-pada*) who are intended here as the primary subjects, not householders.
How does this state of being a novice monk come about for those novices, such that their conduct, when endowed with the status of a novice, will be fully encompassed?
Therefore, according to the principle that "the explanation follows the enumeration," the state of a *śrāmaṇera* itself must first be stated;
thus he says in the verse: "He has gone for refuge. In this context, the meaning of "refuge" (*śaraṇa*) is the sense of protection (*trāṇa*).
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Driven by fear, many people go for refuge to mountains and forests, to groves, shrines, and trees."
From the statement of this verse:
"He went" means he set forth;
"to the Buddha" [is the destination].

Just as one is called "Buddha" because he causes the clusters of lotuses to be drunk upon by swarms of bees who are delighted by all the *karṇikāra* flowers brought forth by the rising rays of the sun, so too the Blessed One is called "Buddha" because he brings about the blossoming of the intellect that knows objects of knowledge liberated from the paths of past, future, and present, and because of the removal of the contraction of delusion. And thus it is said:
"Because of the blossoming of the intellect regarding the objects of knowledge in the three worlds, which are liberated from the [temporal] paths..."
"Or [it means] one who has awakened from or is awakened against the destruction of the contraction of delusion.
Alternatively, a person who has removed sleep and has arisen from sleep is called "awakened" (*vibuddha*).

In the same way, the Blessed One, having arisen from the great bed of *saṃsāra* due to the departure of the sleep of ignorance and through the direct realization of enlightened knowledge (*bauddhajñāna*), is called "Buddha. And so it is said:
"One who has awakened through the cutting off of the sleep of ignorance and the arising of the knowledge of reality is indeed a Buddha, like a person who has woken from sleep. Thus,
he is called "Buddha" because he awakens living beings whose eyes are shrouded by the cataract of the darkness of ignorance.
Alternatively, he is called "Buddha" because he awakens to the auspicious (śiva) by means of unsurpassed knowledge (*anuttara-jñāna*).

Furthermore, it is taught in another treatise that he is established as threefold—by way of the *dharmakāya*, the *sāmbhogikakāya*, and the *nairmāṇikakāya*. For the sake of avoiding excessive prolixity, this is not stated here;
thus, [the term] "Dharma" [is used].
It is called *dharma* because its intrinsic nature is to maintain its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), or because it does not perish;
and it is of two kinds: that which has realization (*adhigama*) as its intrinsic nature, and that which has scripture (*āgama*) as its intrinsic nature.
In this context, "realization" refers to the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣadharmas*), which are infinite and faultless;
"scripture" refers to the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.
Thus, the Dharma is twofold.
Regarding "the Saṃgha":

the four who have entered the path and the four who have attained the fruit—these eight great individuals (mahāpuruṣapudgala) are called the Saṃgha because they constitute the community through their indivisibility.
Who, then, are these eight?

Namely: one who has entered the path for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry is a stream-enterer; one who has entered the path for the realization of the fruit of once-returning is a once-returner;
one who has entered the path for the realization of the fruit of non-returning is a non-returner.
One who has entered the path for the direct realization of the fruit of arhatship is called an "arhat. Thus it is said:
"Because the Buddha, the Dharma, and likewise the Saṅgha cannot be split even by hundreds of millions of Māras, therefore it is designated as 'Saṅgha' (the unbreakable)."
Therefore, the phrase "he who has gone for refuge to that Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha" is to be connected with the words "this novice is [one] in the opinion of the Sage" (SŚ 7).
Since one might occasionally go for refuge even out of fear and so forth, he says:
The meaning is: "by the force of devotion," that is, by the impulse of grace.
Now, for what purpose are the five precepts (*śikṣāpada*) not first taken at the time of giving the refuge (*śaraṇagamana*) and so forth? For he who goes for refuge to him [the Buddha],...
He alone observes his command, and no one else;

therefore, if the five precepts are not first undertaken and the three refuges and so forth are not bestowed, then for one desiring liberation, there would be nothing but contempt for the observance of the precepts.
Therefore, in order that there be no contempt [toward him], and so forth, one should undertake the five precepts by means of taking refuge. *Śikṣā* means training (*śikṣaṇa*).

The meaning is that "practice" (*pratipatti*) or "performance" (*ācaraṇa*) regarding ethical discipline (*śīla*), which consists of engagement and withdrawal, is the actualization of ethical discipline through formal undertaking (*samādāna*). "The fivefold training" (*śikṣā-pañcaka*) means the training itself is fivefold; thus, the sense is "the five [types of] training."
Furthermore, it is called the "Five Precepts" (śikṣāpañcaka) because it conforms to the structure of the verse (kārikā).
What, then, are the precept points (śikṣāpada)?
They are the abstentions from taking life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the occasion of fermented liquors, spirits, and intoxicants.
"Having taken up" means having accepted.
"Who [followed] the Victor?
refers to which person.
"One who has followed forth" means one who has gone forth later. In reference to whom does he say this?
In reference to the Victor (Jina).
He is the Victor (Jina) because he has conquered the afflictions;
he is Upaga because he has conquered the self and evil states;
and he is so called because of the statement in scripture that "it was spoken by the Victor."
The meaning is: he who utters the words, "I follow in renunciation after the Buddha, the Blessed One, who has gone forth."
"Throughout one's life, [one shall abstain from] killing, stealing," and so forth.
By the phrase "throughout one's life," he indicates the limit of time; "killing" (vadhah) means the taking of life (prāṇātipāta), and "stealing" (steyam) means theft (cauryam).
Sexual intercourse is unchaste conduct;
false speech is lying.
Killing, stealing, sexual intercourse, and false speech—these constitute killing, stealing, sexual intercourse, and false speech.
Therefore, what is his [attainment]?
The connection is with the preceding word "one who has desisted" (*virata*).
Is it only from this that one who has desisted is called a "restrained one" (*saṃvara*)? He says: no.
What then? It means also from the drinking of intoxicants (*madyapāna*), that is to say, from the drinking of *surā*, *maireya*, and *madya*.
Now, what is the meaning of "the drinking of *surā*, *maireya*, and *madya*"?
Surā-annāsava is a fermented liquor made from grain; maireya is a fermented liquor made from various substances.
And these two sometimes exist even when the state of being intoxicating (madya) has not yet been reached.
Therefore, there is the mention of "intoxicants" (*madya*). Since betel nuts, *kōdrava* grain, and so forth also cause intoxication, there is the mention of "liquor and spirits" (*surā-maireya*).
[The phrase] "very loudly," and so forth, follows.

It is called a *śayana* because one lies down (*śete*) upon it and falls asleep there; it is called an *āsana* because one sits (*upaviśanti*) upon it. "High" (*mahoccais*) refers to both the bed (*śayana*) and the seat (*āsana*), thus it is a "high bed and seat" (*mahoccaiḥ śayanāsana*).
Therefore, the meaning of "high beds" and "luxurious beds" is as follows:
"nṛtyādeḥ" and so forth;
"nṛtya" means dancing.
Dancing (*nṛtya*) is a dance performed with the flinging out of the arms;
that which is a dance performed by raising both staff-like arms is called *nṛtya*.
Thus it will be stated: "dancing that involves the flinging out of the arms."
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), singing and instrumental music are included;
thus, "dance etc. means dance, song, and instrumental music.
Singing with a loud voice is "song" (*gīta*).
The playing of musical instruments such as the lute (*vīṇā*), the flute (*veṇu*), and the drum (*mṛdaṅga*) is called "instrumental music" (*vāditra*).
Regarding "perfumes, garlands, and so forth": it is called "perfume" (*gandha*) because it is smelled (*gandhyate*); that is the meaning.
In this context, "upayoga" refers to that which is beneficial for a garland; "mālya" refers to flowers such as campaka, aśoka, and so forth. "Ādya" means that which exists at the beginning;
by the word "ādi," the inclusion of ointment (vilepana) is intended.
By that [term], the meaning is perfume, garlands, and ointments.
Ointment (*vilepana*) refers to the smearing of the face with the colors of yellow orpiment and so forth;
it is called "ointment" because it is applied for the purpose of adornment.
Regarding the term "vikālāśana" (eating at the wrong time): here, the period beginning from sunrise up until one *keśa* (the length of a hair) has passed midday is designated by the word "midday.
That afternoon and so forth, during which such a [specific] time has passed, is "vikāla" (the wrong time).
"At that time" means food or eating; the meaning is "from that eating at the wrong time. "In that manner" [is the sense].
By the word "tathā" (likewise), the phrase "who has desisted" is connected;
and by the mention of "gold and silver," *rukma* means gold (*suvarṇa*).
*Rūpya* means silver; the taking of those two is *rūpyarūpyagrahaṇa*.
Therefore, it means "from the acceptance of gold and silver."
"This is the śrāmaṇera according to the Sage's view":
he who abstains from taking life, up to and including the acceptance of gold and silver— he is this śrāmaṇera according to the Sage's view.
"Of the Buddha, the Blessed One" means that which is desired or intended by him.

Although all Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are designated by the general term *muni*— meaning "sage"— due to their silence (*mauna*) of body, speech, and mind, it should nevertheless be understood that the reference here is specifically to the Blessed Śākyamuni.
Because we and others have entered into that teaching, and because the teachings of others have disappeared,
it was not stated as "the doctrine of Śākyamuni" due to a deficiency in the composition of the verse; or, having omitted the word "Śākya," it was indicated as "the doctrine of the Muni."
Just as [one says] "Satyabhāmā" for "Bhāmā.

To put it briefly, this means: having gone for refuge to the Three Jewels and undertaken the five precepts, one utters the words, "I follow after the Buddha, the Blessed One, who has gone forth," and refrains from taking life up to the acceptance of gold and silver.
This very person is considered by the Sage to be a *śrāmaṇera*. Regarding this, it is said: "Having first granted the three refuges and the five precepts..."
One should first remove the hair and then bathe the seeker of the vow.
One should give him the saffron-colored robe and then ordain him;
those who know the Vinaya say that these are the ten precepts.
Now, the means for becoming a novice (śrāmaṇera) is explained. He begins the summary of the conduct of these novices with the words,
"with his entire body," and so forth.
In this context, it is called the *śarīra* because the limbs (*aṅga*) wither (*śīryante*) within it;
and since even a certain part [of the body] could be so designated, the term "entire" (*sakala*) is employed.
Thus, the meaning is "with the whole body" (*kāyena*), that is, by means of the entire body in every respect.
"Or by one part of the body" means by one [member] of the collection such as the hand, foot, head, and so forth— namely, by the hand or other [limb].
That which is grasped by a limb of the body, such as a hand or foot, is that which is connected to the body.
The meaning is "with a creeper-stick distinct from his own body.
He should not strike, that is, he should not kill. To whom? He says:
A "living being" (prāṇin): that which is called "vital breath" (prāṇa) is wind;
one who possesses this is a living being.
And what specifically is that [body]?
It is understood as that which has been produced from the five branches and so forth;
therefore, there is no abandonment of the vow (*saṃvara*) when the *kalala* and subsequent stages are destroyed.
Moreover, by the word "living being" (prāṇin), only a synonym for the human realm is intended, and not all living beings whatsoever,
because of the statement regarding the fault in using water containing insects and so forth;
or else, this word denotes a genus.
Therefore, for one who kills a woman, a man, or a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch), or [a being] produced from the five limbs and so forth, there would certainly be a loss of restraint (*saṃvara*).
By this verse, physical prowess is prohibited.
He states the phrase prohibiting verbal transgression:
"The color of death," and so forth.
Death is the cessation of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
"His praise" means his commendation;
"he should not speak it" means he should not utter it.
"You have performed meritorious deeds; hearing that your journey to the park is actually your departure for the next world, someone might kill themselves.
Therefore, it is now prohibited here because it involves the abandonment of restraint preceded by an evil deed."
"One should not speak of the color of death,
nor should one seek out a 'weapon-bearer' (śastrahāra).
One who carries or bears a weapon is a "weapon-bearer," that is, an executioner.
In that regard, one should investigate:
by means of a killer, with the intention to kill,
by means of the mind, and by means of the mental faculty.
One should not employ [it] for the purpose of killing or for the sake of causing death.
Demonstrating that the abandonment of the vow occurs even for one who kills by means of other applications besides the previously mentioned synonyms, he says:
"By purgation, emesis, ointment," and so forth.
In this context, "purgation" refers to causing vomiting.
Vamana is emesis;
when there is a change in color due to an ointment, it perishes.
Poison is both natural and artificial.
"Weapon" refers to the thunderbolt and so forth;
"purgative," "emetic," and "ointment," etc., form a dvandva compound.
The preparation of these is their "processing" (*abhisaṃskṛti*).
One should not perform that;
for what reason? For the sake of killing living beings, for the purpose of human slaughter, and not for the destruction of the fetus.
The meaning is that one should not perform an abortion;
some explain this as the locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*), stating that one should not perform purgation or similar acts for the purpose of causing an abortion.
Demonstrating that not only is it impossible to kill by this practice, but even merely to create the cause for death is not easily accomplished, he says:
"The observer of the vow should not make a sign," and so forth.
"Sign" (nimitta) means a mark (liṅga); he should not make one.
Who would not do this? He says:
the one observing the vow (vratī).
By what means? By the cries of owls and other such animals heard during sleep.
Regarding "dream," there are five types of dreams;
for it is said that the fivefold dream, which is called "truth" because it is practiced infinitely through the falsity of dreaming,
belongs to birds such as owls.
"Vāśitāni" means weeping; and "dreams" refers to the howling of owls and other such creatures. By these [means].
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of giving names, lineages, and so forth.
That [giving] is threefold, distinguished by the categories of Dharma, material goods (āmiṣa), and fearlessness (abhaya).
Material giving (āmiṣadāna) is also twofold, distinguished by the categories of external and internal.

Immorality is the abandoning of morality. Morality consists in the undertaking of ethical conduct that is refreshing—due to its cooling of the heat of suffering and its freedom from remorse—and so forth; for it is stated in a verse: "The body does not suffer [when one has undertaken morality]. It is called *śīla* because it attains (*lāti*) a state of coolness (*śīta-bhāva*) through the sequence leading to *nirvāṇa*. This includes both natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and conventional offenses (*prajñapti-sāvadya*), such as eating at improper times, which have been prohibited by the Blessed One.
There are four fruits: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship.
The attainment of these fruits is their acquisition.
Giving, morality, and the attainment of the fruits—these are "giving, morality, and the attainment of the fruits."
Therefore, the connection is with the words "by those [thoughts].
To show that even for one who kills through a murderous mind out of delusion, there is no loss of the vow (*saṃvara*), he says:
"among those preceded by the middle, the last, and the first," and so forth.

"Those who go in the middle, behind, or in front" are called *madhyapaścātpurogāḥ*. Therefore, while those people who are going in the middle, behind, or in front are moving along, "wherever the murderous mind [is directed]"— that is, toward whichever person the intent to kill is focused— killing or slaying that very person,
"of this one" refers to the novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*).
Violence (*hiṃsā*) is the killing of a living being.
The meaning is that for one who kills another person in error, mistaking him for someone else, there is no violence (*hiṃsā*) on his part.
Who says this?
Therefore he says:
"The All-Knowing" (sarvavit);
one who knows everything is the All-Knowing.
"The Blessed One is the Buddha; he spoke thus"—by this, he demonstrates the authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*).
Showing that no other ritual application (prayoga) should be performed for the purpose of killing,
he says "kūṭa," etc.
They describe *kūṭa* as a snare (*pāśa*).
"Avamārtha" refers to a snare-mechanism;
"avaṣṭambha" refers to a mechanism by which one may strike after suddenly attacking.
They describe *avapāya* as a precipice.
A *vetāla* is the entry of piśācas and the like into a corpse through the power of mantras by means of ministers.
*Abhisaṃskṛti* is the preparation of counterfeit objects and so forth.
And by causing her to fall [into the fire], what would he not do for the sake of killing embodied beings?
Otherwise, however, there is no fault.
They call a *kūṭaka* a "noose" (*pāśa*), a snare-mechanism for the purpose of capturing; and an *avapaya* or *avapā* is that very mechanism known as a "post" (*stambha*).
Thus is the summary verse.
To show that one cannot even obtain instruction regarding a place for the sake of death,
he says "taskara" and so forth.
"Taskara" means a thief or robber.
*Ahiḥ* means a serpent.
*Senā* is a gathering together for the purpose of battle.
The remainder is easy to understand.
A renunciant should not describe the path—that route on which there is danger from thieves and the like—to embodied beings, that is, to living creatures, for the sake of their destruction or ruin.
To show that he is not even able to cross over the crossing of the treacherous river,
he says "bhujaga," and so forth.
A *bhujaga* is a serpent, because it moves by means of its arms (*bhujābhyām*).
"Āvarta," "vegin," "bhujaga," and "āvartaka" form a dvandva compound; [the word] "bhayam" refers to the fear of those.
Wherever there may be danger at the bathing place of any river, one should not reveal that bathing place.

Furthermore, he says "something to kings," etc., in order to show that one is not capable of having another person killed by means of prohibiting the giving of punishment and so forth, [thinking] that one should not reveal the path where a king might execute someone.
"Bhū" means the earth.
One who protects that [earth] is a *bhūpati*, a king.
"Do not give even a little to the *bhūpati*, the king"—the meaning is: "You shall not give even the slightest amount of wealth."
"Better to give up life"—the meaning is: "You should choose the abandonment of life.
Some say that one should not speak such improper or unsuitable words in the presence of a person who is intent on receiving a fitting gift.
But the Venerable Parahitaghoṣa says:
"One who is appointed to every task on all sides is called *āyukta*, that is, one who is occupied;
another person who is bound or obstructed by such an *āyukta* should not be referred to as 'bound to the *āyukta* person'."
"It would be better for you to die than to give any property to the king.
Otherwise, the meaning—as before—is that one should not say of a person who is obstructed and occupied [with other matters] that he is "bound" or "engaged" [in a legal suit].
Otherwise, it would have been said: "It would be better for you to die than to give anything to one who is unrighteous (*ayukta*)."
It is not [the case that] kings [are meant], because they have been excluded by those appointed [to the task], nor any other person, because he is bound.
Showing that it is not permissible to point out a shelter that is dangerous with a murderous intent, he says "bhujaga... and so forth.
Here, by the word *vihāra*, only a shelter (*layana*) is meant, on the grounds that they dwell (*viharanti*) within it.
From this, the following meaning of the sentence arises:
(SŚ 14) One should not assign a dwelling in which there is danger from snakes and the like to a visiting monk who is likely to be killed by them.
For one who does so assign it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*), provided that death does not occur.
However, at death, there occurs the abandonment of the restraint.
To demonstrate that even by designating someone as a "cat" or the like, one who kills an enemy becomes a non-recluse (ayati), he says:
"By designating him as a tiger," and so forth.
A novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*) of deceitful nature who, having made the designation "I shall kill a tiger," should kill an enemy, must be expelled from the monastery (*vihāra*).
"Quickly" means swiftly;
"he should be expelled by the novices" should be understood to mean when the enemy has died.
He also prohibits the performance of unrighteous acts with the words "it should be done in such a way," and so forth;
that is, it should be performed in such a manner that not even a single enemy or foe remains alive.
In this way, [he addresses] the enemies, the foes.
Restraint: an unrighteous action is not to be performed;
one should not engage in the practice of unrighteous conduct.
"Recalling [the body] as being like a saw":
that which is compared to a saw (*krakaca*), that is, to a mechanical instrument for cutting, when one is dead, is described in this way.
Recalling what, then?
The connection is that one should not perform unrighteous actions.
He shows that even by employing another to kill, one becomes a transgressor,
starting with the words "by killing," and so forth.
If one, two, or even three novices are made the targets [of an act] with the intention of killing them simultaneously at one and the same time,
that constitutes the preliminary effort (*prayoga*).
If one causes a human being to be killed through the instigation of a novice monk (śrāmaṇera),
those [monks] are to be expelled from the monastery.
Demonstrating that the killing of a human being occurs through these factors and exhorting others [to understand this], he says:
"The undertaking," and so forth.
In this context, "the undertaking" refers to the grasping of weapons and the like.

The notion "this is a human being" is the notion of a person (*nṛ-saṃjñā*). Sometimes one employs a stratagem while possessing the notion of a person, yet he says, "This is not a human being," [but rather] "a man" (*nara*).
If that person is human,
these three factors may sometimes occur,
but not the intention to kill.
Therefore, there is the statement regarding the intention to kill:
sometimes an undertaking is perceived,
and the person possesses both the perception of a human and the intention to kill.
But it does not deprive one of life;
therefore, he says:
"and the exhaustion of life."
"Commencing with that" is the first limb;
"the designation 'man'" is the second limb;
and "'human being'" is the third limb.

The fourth factor is the intention to kill, and the fifth factor is the destruction of life; these five factors are to be understood as constituting the killing of a human being, that is, the murder of a person.
However, some of dull intellect say:
They read "nare vadhaka-cetanā" with the word ending in the locative case.
For them, the five factors are not established, because the phrase "nare vadhaka-cetanā" constitutes only a single factor;
furthermore, the Vinaya is thereby subverted by them.
For this is the instruction in the Vinaya:
there is a living being,
and one perceives it as a living being.
When a murderous intent has arisen,
one carries out the assault,
and the other is deprived of life, by this much one becomes a perpetrator of taking life.

And here, in the passage beginning with "there is a living being," every term is indicated in the nominative case. Likewise, in another verse, in the phrase "the commencement" and "the consciousness of the killer who perceives [the victim] as a human," the nominative case is employed.
Therefore, it should be understood that the indication is exclusively in the nominative case.
Showing that one is not even authorized to kill by means of employing poison, weapons, and so forth, he says:
"The novice monk," and so on.
Whatever poison, weapon, or the like is employed by an ascetic for the destruction of a person...
If a person dies by that very same application [of the lethal act], then the perpetrator falls from his restraint (saṃvara) due to the lack of restraint (asaṃvara).
But if it is by another's [application], then it is not so; by this, he explains that no transgression occurs for him.
"Such as one who has been purchased," and so forth:
this ascetic may have been purchased by someone, or he may be a hired servant; because of such [status], he is ignorant of discipline (*vinaya*).

Furthermore, even one who knows the Vinaya might kill a person because of a lapse of memory; by the word "etcetera," it is meant that due to being overcome by hatred, one might kill a person thinking that there is no loss of restraint for those such as slaves who have been purchased.
One who kills becomes a transgressor of the vows,
but not one who is insane and so forth.
However, novice monks who kill those with deranged or distracted minds do not become possessed of immoral conduct, because of the absence of mindfulness.
He states the cause for the action of harming sentient beings with the words beginning "kāya" (body), etc. It is called *karuṇā* because it obstructs (*ruṇaddhi*) suffering (*ka*).
Those who exist within that state are compassionate;
for indeed, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, suffer from the suffering of others.

Therefore, those compassionate ones—by a striving novice monk—must always, at all times, perform friendly physical action, friendly verbal action, and friendly mental action toward living beings and sentient creatures.
"Thus spoken" means so stated; "because" (yasmāt) means for which reason; from this cause just mentioned, he asks: "What [is the result]? and says:
"One should not harm sentient beings" is the verse. One should not inflict suffering upon sentient beings. By what means? He says:
By means of wooden, rope, and leather bindings;
therein, "wood" refers to timber,
and "rope" refers to a cord made of fibers.
Iron is metal; leather is a binding material; their fastenings are made from these.
"Anala" means fire;
"jala" means water. "Jalānala" refers to both water and fire. Immersing oneself therein is "entry into water and fire."
"Non-renunciation" (*an-uttyāga*) refers to the non-abandonment of what has been renounced.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the author] includes such acts as consuming poison.
"Entering water or fire" and "non-renunciation" form a copulative compound (*dvandva*).
One should not employ him in that.
Regarding the passage beginning with "kṛmigorūpa" (worms, cows, forms, etc.):
since the harming of worms, cattle, forms, and so forth, as well as wrong livelihood, occurs when there is cultivation, for that reason one should abandon cultivation from afar.
One should not brand cows, buffaloes, and so forth; cows, buffaloes,
and so forth must not be branded, nor should one pierce the nostrils of these cows, buffaloes, and so forth.
And one should not strike him with a cane or similar object.
"Intending," and so forth: having intended for a *śrāmaṇera*, one should deprive a fish or similar creature of its life;
having deprived it of life, for the ascetic who eats the condiment made from its meat, a heart that is merciless and pitiless arises toward that *śrāmaṇera*.
Therefore, one who eats meat prepared specifically for him may, being filled with the fire of greed, even commit the killing of living beings; thus, violence is possible for such a person.
Consequently, the intention is that one should not eat meat prepared specifically for oneself.
He explains how that which is done for its sake is to be understood, saying:
"But it should be known by three aspects," and so forth.
That which is done for its sake should be understood as being performed with regard to something that has been perceived without error, heard, or suspected.
Desiring to provide the definition of these very terms, he says:
"That which is seen by oneself" and so forth. That which has been seen by oneself is called *īkṣita*.
But that which is spoken by one who is trustworthy and non-deceptive is called "heard" (śruta).
With reference to doubt, he says:
"Bound in the house," and so forth.

From seeing the wings, horns, and so on of those birds, deer, pigs, and others that are bound in the house, a doubt arises as to whether these deer, birds, pigs, and so forth have been killed for one's sake or not.
When there is doubt, the donor should be questioned: "Were these killed for my sake or not?
Thus questioned, the donor says, "I am the giver," and so forth.
When the donor, being thus questioned, speaks in this way: "These deer and others were killed on your account, for your sake."

This being the case, one should not eat in that house; the implication is that it was prepared specifically for him. By the phrase "abstaining from the killing of living beings," he shows that this prohibition applies to one who has undertaken the training rules, and not to anyone else.
"Or killed by hawks and the like," and so forth.
Now, that donor might think:
"These birds have been killed, slain by hawks and other predators."
Whether they die from eating rice, barley, or mung beans,
or are killed for the sake of their parents or for a sacrifice— such being the case, there is no fault in those who eat.
The meaning is that when the giver speaks thus, no fault whatsoever accrues to those who partake.
"Intended for one Śrīghana," and so forth:
if fish or other meat, or a side dish, has been prepared specifically for one śrāmaṇera, it is not permissible for the use of other śrāmaṇeras or ascetics (yatins).
Furthermore, that which has been prepared intending it for monks (bhikṣus), nuns (bhikṣuṇīs), laymen (upāsakas), or laywomen (upāsikās) is also not permissible for their consumption.
"Water from rivers and so forth" means: that which originates in a river is *nādeya*;
what is it? Water.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), ponds and the like are included.
Of what nature [is it]? It is "containing living beings," meaning containing animate creatures. Even knowing that it contains animate creatures, one should not drink it.
Who would not drink? The text says:
"the one observing the vow," because of the word "knowing."

There is no fault in ignorance [of this]. Here, the word "living beings" (*jantu*) does not include fish and the like, because they possess the capacity for discernment; rather, "living beings" here are intended to be subtle organisms.
"Beings" refers to living creatures;
"subtle" means invisible.
In this context, within this training precept (*śikṣāpada*), these are what is intended.
To the question "What are they like?", he says:
"The *trasikarā*, the *ūrmikarā*, and so forth";
that is to say, [beings] such as the *ūrmikara* and the rest.
Now, for what purpose is this verse established separately?

For, in the verse "One should perform the watering of trees and the bathing of the guru with water that is not impure," the prohibition against watering trees and so forth with water containing living beings is already understood;
indeed, where the watering itself is prohibited, the prohibition against drinking [such water] is all the more certain.
This is true in a secondary sense, but not in a primary one.
Here, there is no intention to kill by means of the mouth's form, because the primary aim is the desire to drink;
therefore, this verse has been established separately.
Furthermore, there is no fault in not having it written down due to the power of the arising of the meaning; this is because the Vinaya possesses the power of the arising of its meaning.
Regarding "water" and so forth: one should place a water-vessel (*dharmaka-raṅka*) together with a filter (*khalaka*) in order to purify the water.
"At the very least, even the treasury should be empowered"—the meaning is that it should be consecrated.
To the question "Whose treasury is to be empowered? he says:
"That of one who is well-attired."
The meaning is "of the good cloth.
For what purpose? To avoid obstacles.
And the phrase "to avoid misdeeds" is to be supplied [as an additional purpose].
"Divyanetra," and so forth.
That which exists in heaven (*divi*) is "divine" (*divya*).
What is that? It is the eye (*netra*), the organ of sight (*cakṣus*).
One who possesses divine eyes is "divyanetra.
One who is blind is "cakṣurindriyarahita" (devoid of the faculty of sight).
For a śrāmaṇera who is both divyanetra and blind, it is not desired—that is, it was not stated.
What is it that is not desired? He says:
the examination of water.
First of all, the prohibition against a blind person examining water is reasonable, because of his lack of capacity.
Now, why is there a prohibition regarding the divine eye (*divyanetra*)?
For that [eye] perceives even those living beings residing on the earth who are subtle, internal, or of an invisible form.
Therefore, it is said: the prohibition of the divine eye is for the purpose of removing doubt.
The Venerable Prajñāsiṃha said: "Those with the divine eye are called 'of inferior intellect,' because of the nature of such a form;
there would be no discernment for ordinary worldlings."
Therefore, it is for the purpose of making a prohibition.
But surely, because a blind person lacks the capacity for examining water, such an examination will not occur anyway;
what is the use of this prohibition?
Those who know the Vinaya explain that the prohibition is due to the possibility of seeing one whose eyes are clear.
He asks, "By whom, then, should the water be inspected? and replies with the words beginning with "hand" (*hasta*).
One whose habit it is to see the *āvarta*—that is, the subtle lines—on the tip of the thumb of the hand is described as such.
It is not prevented;
that is to say, it is unpreventable.
By this very [statement], they refute those who suffer from ophthalmia.
Regarding how long one who observes the whorls at the back of the hand should continue the examination, he says:
"Of the eyes," and so forth.
Thinking, "Let there be no wandering of the eyes," one should not look for a long time—that is, for a great duration—nor should one gaze fixedly.
"No" is the negation;
"that" refers to the water.
He says that it must be examined precisely because of the long-standing prohibition.
"One should certainly not act for even a moment," and so forth.
*Māyā* is the deceiving of others;
*śāṭhya* is crookedness of mind by which one does not reveal what is as it is, but instead behaves in an obscure manner.
Deceit (*māyā*) and guile (*śāṭhya*) constitute "deceit-and-guile.
Therefore, he is endowed with those two.
For the sake of merely forming a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*), he does not need to perform such analytical investigation (*pratyavekṣaṇīya*).
He says that a restriction of time must then be made:
"by which interval," and so forth; until, after an interval of time, sixty years—that is, sixty years—have passed, the elephant, the beast, wanders about.
The meaning is that such a duration of time is as long as it takes for a cart filled with bamboo to complete its revolution;
this is to be understood as the "observation of water" (salilekṣaṇa), that is, the observation of water.
"Upward," and so forth: upward, downward, and middle constitute "upward-downward-middle.
What are these three? They are the stages (bhūmi).
Of what? Of water.
"Whichever ground attains purity" means that among these three grounds, whichever ground attains purity becomes free from living beings.
One should perform the ritual action with that [earth];
the connection is "with that earth."
Regarding the passage beginning with "yatra":
in whatever river or pond large, massive creatures, when struck by the palm of the hand— that is, struck by the hand— go downward to dry land, there one should take water.
"If it is not to be poured out":
the word *cet* has the sense of "if.
If, when struck by the palms of the hands, living beings do not go downward, then that water should be poured out.
By what? By the five-fingered [hand];
that is to say, by the five fingers.
"There would be water," and so forth.
In water where living beings cling to the hand and emerge, a renunciant (yati) should not wash his hands, feet, face, clothes, or other such items therein.
"Face" (āsya) means the mouth;
it is not analyzed [separately] because it is easy to understand.
"In the family," and so forth.
If a novice monk has been invited to a meal at a household, he should go there and ask: "Has water been poured out here or not?
If [the answer] is "no," it is designated as *saṃjñika*.
One should say, "Make it flow.
If, when asked, the donor says, "It has not been made to flow," then one should say to the designated person:
One who possesses perception (*saṃjñā*) is called "possessed of perception" (*saṃjñika*); it is precisely such a person who is intended here.
He who is skilled in causing [the semen] to flow is the one who should be addressed.
"What is this? [he asked].
"Drain this water containing living beings," [the other replied].
But the other did not.
He who is more senior and does not know how to filter [the water] should not be told, "Filter it.
If he says so, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If even a single person is not skilled in causing [the candidate] to hear [the precepts], then what should be done? To this he says:
"But one must bathe," and so forth.
From a strainer:

having poured water containing living beings into one's own bowl, if asked from where this water was brought, one should pour it back into that very place—such as the lotus pond—from which it was taken; one should do this oneself so that the salt water, which causes harm to living beings, does not reach another location. Thus he says "into that very place."
"Or for seven days," and so forth.
Alternatively, wherever water remains for seven days, there that water containing living beings should be discarded;
or else, one should place it in a cauldron or similar vessel within the monastery.
To the question "Of what kind is it?", he says: "It does not dry up"; that water does not undergo desiccation there.
While that [water] has not yet dried up, one should place it in a cauldron or similar vessel.
Some explain the locative case in "while that has not dried up" as a *nimitta-saptamī* (locative of cause), meaning "for the purpose of not drying up the water.
Regarding the passage beginning with "when it has rained," etc.:
Or rather, when it has rained even more profusely upon the god [the cloud]. Of what sort? Carrying a torrent of clear water; "clear" means unclouded.

The sense is that it has the nature (*śīla*) of carrying a flood of water, a torrent of water; thus, it carries a clear flood of water. When such rain has fallen, one should say, "May those waters containing living beings go to the lord of rivers, the great ocean," and then release them.
Now, if all this is not possible,
and there is a water-drinking station where the water has come from a great distance,
then he says what should be done with that water containing living beings:
"Extremely long," and so forth:
the lower part of her feet is exceedingly long;
her face—that is, her mouth—is long, and she possesses two cords.
That vessel being thus bound is called a *ghaṭikā*;
by means of it, one who has traveled a great distance should release that water into a well from below.
He explains how a traveler should proceed regarding water:
"For three *ghaṭikās*.
Having observed for three *ghaṭikās*, the one traveling on the road should drink water from a well or a water-pit.
Is it even when they are completely pure? No, he says.
What then? "If all of them are completely pure, then it may be drunk.
The word *cet* has the sense of *yadi* (if).
If those three *ghaṭikās* are completely pure, then, while reflecting upon them, it should be drunk by this path;
otherwise, it must be discharged.
How otherwise?
If those three *ghaṭikās* are not purified,
then water containing living organisms must be drained away.
"Having observed for three *ghaṭikās*": some say this means observing the water contained within three *ghaṭikās*, that is,
observing the water drop by drop.
"Once" means just once. Others say it means "having observed each [breath] little by little.
However, this [latter interpretation] alone is logical.

Furthermore, it is appropriate to consider that "one should examine even a small amount" according to the verse stating, "there are three regions of water—above, below, and in the middle. However, this does not apply to every single rule of training (*śikṣāpada*), because of the statement: "knowing [the water] to be from a river or the like. Therefore, permission is granted to examine even a mere *ghaṭikā* (a small measure) as being "only a small amount."
The same applies here as well:

if it is argued that in that case [of the previous example] only a small portion was [taken] because it was impossible, whereas here everything is [taken] because it is possible; [then we reply: so be it.

If that is so, then let there simply be no investigation in that case because it is impossible. Or, if mental purification is prescribed even when something is impossible by means of a small amount [of effort],
why is it not likewise done for every single training rule (*śikṣāpada*) when it is possible?
Based on the statement, "Knowing the water of rivers and the like," therefore,
even when asked, only a small amount should be examined.
Some read the text as, "having looked at [the water] for five *ghaṭikās*."
Since those [other texts] have a different purpose, their reading should not be accepted; rather,
the injunction there concerns a period of six or five *ghaṭikās* beyond the time for traveling.
They should be enjoyed after careful examination; otherwise, one incurs a transgression.
"Not a rope and a water-pot," and so forth:
"rope" (rajjū) and "water-pot" (ghaṭikā) form the compound *rajjughaṭike*; the giving or relinquishing of these two is not praised, nor is it approved.
He asks, "Where? and says: "In water containing living beings.
Water that exists together with living beings is "water containing living beings" (*saprāṇaka*); [it is] in that.
Is that alone not recommended? No, he says.
What then? "To say 'drink,' etc.
A mendicant is never at any time permitted to say or give water containing living beings to another, saying, "Drink!"
Just as this which was immediately mentioned [above] should not be done by an ascetic,
he says "containing living beings" and so forth to show that one should not even say, "This pond and so on contains living beings."
One should not speak loudly to others, saying, "This lotus pond, river, or tank contains living beings.
However, if someone asks, "What is this? [one may explain].
One should give a reply such as,
"It contains living beings," in the case of a pond or similar body of water;
then, having examined it, one may decide whether or not to carry out the work.

When questioned, he should answer others after having inspected them; "perform the water-rite"—this being the case, when questioned, the ascetic (yati) should say what [is present] regarding the other [beings], but he should not say that there are living beings (saprāṇaka). This is the meaning.
The meaning is that this is for the sake of avoiding public reproach.
And just as one should not speak in such a manner toward others, one might ask: "Should one do so even toward preceptors and teachers? He says: "No."
"What then, Preceptor? and so forth:
one must clearly state whether this pond and such contain living beings or not;
one must speak to one's own preceptors and teachers, and must not act with deceit.

If that is so, then since drinking water containing living beings is prohibited for oneself and giving [such water] to others is prohibited, would not the giving of food and the watering of insentient things such as trees be unrestricted?
To dispel the doubt that these might be external objects of enjoyment, he says:
"Watering trees," and so forth.
One should not water trees with impure water;
one should not even perform the ritual bathing of preceptors and teachers—by this, external enjoyment is prohibited.
But would water alone, when rendered containing living beings, not make a sickle curved?
Or is it something else as well?
He says: "It is something else as well."
"Curd-whey vinegar," and so forth.
By the word *mastu*, curd-whey (*dadhimastu*) is meant;
*kāñjika* and "grain-water" (*dhānyāmbu*) have the same meaning.
Sauvīra is prepared from many medicinal substances and specific waters;
maṇḍa is a derivative of food;
daṇḍāhata is churned [with a staff].
Therefore, a renunciant should not drink such water containing living beings, nor should he give it to another,
nor should he discard it upon the earth.
"Infested with bugs," and so forth: a bed that is inhabited by bugs should not be dried in the sun;
nor should it be cast into snow, mud, cold water, or hot water.
By this, he prohibits even the mere act of causing pain to sentient beings.
Regarding "new construction" and so forth:
a mendicant should not perform new construction on a shrine, grove, monastery, or the like using water containing living beings;
by implication, it is stated that it must be done after having drained [the water].
Having drained that water until the end of the day—not throughout the entire day—one must hold the triangular strainer; "must be held" is the meaning.
However, from time to time, it should be released for draining, in order to avoid causing pain to living beings and to avoid committing an offense.
Now, regarding how one who causes another to recite should proceed, he says:
"He should train the hired laborer in this way," and so forth.
A practitioner should instruct the worker in this manner.
"What is it? "Bind a triangle. "Laborer, tie the strap!"
"Just as one draws water from a well, so should one cause it to flow out;
so should one release the bucket."
If that water, even while being strained, remains containing living organisms, then what should be done? To this he says:
"With seven triangles," and so forth. (SŚ 25)
If that water, while being strained through a single-layered cloth filter, is not purified,
then it should be strained through a seven-layered cloth filter;
if even in this way the water is not purified, [it must be discarded].
Then an investigation must be conducted;
if she is not cleared,
then one should abandon the new construction and go to another region.
This means that one must go from that location to another location.
When, then, should new construction work be undertaken? To this he says:
"Arising after having not existed," and so forth.
For these living beings, appearing in the form of insects, come into existence after not having existed,
and having existed, they subsequently perish.
When these living beings, having come into existence, pass from one state of being to another birth, [they do so].
Then, the new construction work (navakarma) should be undertaken.
By whom? By one who acts according to the prescribed rules (yathoktavidhikārī). One whose habit it is to perform the prescribed rules of conduct is "one who acts according to the prescribed rules."
The word "tena" (by that) constitutes the connection.
Regarding the phrase "satpaṭa" and so forth: a beautiful cloth is a *satpaṭa*.
From that which is bound with it—the support for the bowl (*dhāraṇapātraka*) situated on a bed or stool—from that [it is prohibited].
From what kind [of vessel]? From one that is four finger-breadths high.
Water should be taken from a river or similar body of water from a bed or other such object whose height is four finger-breadths;
having looked and examined it.
"Regarding new construction": this means for the purpose of new construction.

What is meant is as follows: in rivers, ponds, and the like, having fashioned a frame for a bed or stool, and having wrapped a water-vessel with a thick cloth, having placed stones or similar objects inside, having submerged it in the water, and having made it rise four finger-breadths above [the surface], the water contained within that—
Having examined it, the water-related task should be performed.
"Having two pierced ears," and so forth.
A thread that is attached— that is, tied— to two pierced wooden ears is "the thread attached to the two pierced ears."
That which is bound by two sticks—that is, fastened between a pair of sticks—is called a *dhāraṇapātraka*.
Such a *dhāraṇapātraka* should be placed externally at the bottom of the triangular *khalaka*.
"With a mind pervaded by compassion," and so forth.
A practitioner whose mind is thus "pervaded"—meaning completely encompassed—by *kṛpā*, that is, by compassion (*karuṇā*), is described as such.

By that compassionate Śrīghana, sweet and delicious water—that is, drinking water containing living beings or organisms—must not be released, nor must it be cast away, into alkaline water, that is, into salty water.

But for one who releases [the water] without compassion, there is an offense; this applies to one who perceives it as pure when it is not pure. However, for one who perceives alkaline water as pure and intends it to be pure, there is no offense.
It is neither an offense nor a non-offense;
the meaning is that it does not constitute a *duṣkṛta*.

In this regard, beginning with "with the entire body" and extending through "one who has been hired," these other verses describe the abandonment of the vow (*saṃvara*) preceded by a misdeed (*duṣkṛta*).
By the remaining [verses], the misdeeds themselves are illustrated.
Here, there exists a human body endowed with volition (*cetanā*), and therein lies the intention to kill.
How could restraint not be abandoned by one who possesses the consciousness of killing a killer?
Thus ends the riddle.
In the *Sphuṭārthā*, the commentary on the *Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha*, the first chapter, titled "The Precept on Abstinence from Taking Life," is completed.
The training rule characterized by abstaining from the killing of living beings has been explained.
Now, the training rule regarding abstaining from taking what is not given must be stated,
for it is held that by the theft of even the slightest thing belonging to anyone, one ceases to be a śramaṇa.
Therefore, pointing out the variety of high and low [levels],
he says "kālika" and so forth;
here, the word *kāla* (time) is employed.

"One who observes the vow does not tolerate the enjoyment of food and drink" refers to food, drink, and so forth that are restricted to specific times; and "time" here refers to the third part of the night.
That which is fit for as long as one lives is "lifelong" (*yāvajjīvika*), such as long pepper (*pippalī*) and the like.

That which, once accepted, is permitted for seven days for a monk who has mastered the *śrīghanas* [meditative concentrations] is "seven-day" (*sāptāhika*), such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and the like.
Although it will be stated later that "seven-day" refers to clarified butter and so forth, it is mentioned here in accordance with the requirements of the verse composition.
"Parihārya" means that which deserves to be avoided; it refers to the robes and other requisites of an ascetic, meaning they are capable of being carried.
By the phrase "of that which is not to be taken up," and so forth, it indicates that because it is heavy in nature, it is a "heavy object" (gurudravya) belonging exclusively to the Saṅgha.
It is not any other heavy object, because it is intended specifically as a heavy object belonging to the Saṅgha;
one is able to touch and handle it,
but not to lift it up.

Therefore, items such as pearls are "allowable" (kalpya), while gold and the like are "unallowable" (akalpika) because they are incapable of even being touched. Thus it will be stated: "One should not take another's property, whether it be allowable or unallowable, for as long as one is observing the vow."
The eight requisites have been explained;
now the sixteen are being stated:
"earth, water," and so forth.
"Earth and water," and so forth, form a copulative compound (dvandva).
Among these, the substance "earth" is the source for the production of gold and the like;
the substance "two-footed beings" refers to humans and so forth.
Four-footed substances include buffaloes and the like;
legless substances include serpents and the like;
and footed substances include mango trees and the like.
The phrase "and those things" (tadatam) means that which exists starting from the earth and ending with trees.
In this context, there are eight requisites beginning with the earth and ending with trees;
and there are another eight consisting of those very things, making sixteen in total.
The word "and" (*ca*) is used for the purpose of indicating the aforementioned meaning through conjunction.
"One should not take" (*nādadīta*) means one should not seize.
"Another's property" (*parasvaka*) means the wealth of another.
By these eight and sixteen substances, the inclusion of all substances is accomplished.
Since the inclusion of all substances is thus established by the sixteen substances alone, for what purpose are the eight requisites, such as the seasonal robes and so forth, mentioned separately?
This is true.

However, having extracted [certain items] from those very sixteen substances, eight refinements (*pariṣkāra*) are specified separately for the purpose of demonstrating, without confusion, their status as *kālika* (timely) and so forth. Furthermore, the specification of *kālika* and the rest must necessarily be made in order to demonstrate that the Saṃgha of the four directions who have spent the rains retreat and are present [at the ceremony] partakes of them as appropriate.
And for this reason, eight [items] are specified separately.
In the same way, sixteen requisites should be mentioned for walls and so forth.
How are they eight?
This is true;
however, the eight were mentioned first for the purpose of establishing the sequence of the numbers eight and sixteen.
This is the summarized meaning.
"One should not take up nor accept the eight requisites, beginning with land";
thus the sixteen and eight requisites have been explained. Now, he states at what measure of theft of these materials the abandonment of the vow (*saṃvara*) occurs:
"Four parts of a kārṣāpaṇa," and so forth.
Here, by the word *kārṣāpaṇa*, nineteen copper coins (*kapardaka-pana*) are intended.
Its fourth part consists of five *māṣakas* less one *kākinī*; taking these away [constitutes the offense].

Alternatively, if a novice (śrāmaṇera), with the intent to steal— that is, with the intention of theft— takes, displaces from its place, or appropriates wealth such as cloth or other items worth half that [value], he should be swiftly expelled by the other renunciants; the meaning is that he should be seized and turned out of the door.
The measure of the substance has been stated.
From what point, then, does one who steals that substance cease to be a śrāmaṇera? To this he says:
"If [it is] enclosed," and so forth.
When an elephant is being led away while situated within an enclosure with four gates, if the gates are wide open,
then there is no transgression (*ayati*) when the elephant has passed through with all four feet;
however, if the gates are closed, [there is a transgression].
Then, when he has gone out, there would be a "dvipahṛt.
One who drinks with two [trunks] is a *dvipa*, meaning an elephant;
one who carries away (*harati*) that [elephant] is a *dvipahṛt*.
The meaning is that one would become a thief of elephants.
Thus, by this verse, two locations are established: first, the feet are the location when the gate is wide open; second, the enclosure (vāṭa) is the location when the gate is closed.
"Ankle," and so forth:
the ankle is a joint of the foot;
"in that" refers to something such as a stalk of sugarcane tied there.
Of what kind?
Drawn far away, meaning led to a distance;
lifted up, meaning raised.
Why? From the surface of the earth— that is, from the ground—
does the breaking of the restraint, meaning the abandonment of the restraint, occur?
"Like an elephant from a cage, O twice-born one":

just as it is said that for an elephant, even the mere lifting of a foot constitutes the abandonment of its confinement when the gate and enclosure are large, whereas [the confinement is lost] only when it has actually exited through a small door;

likewise, in the case of a cage, even the mere lifting of a foot constitutes [the loss of confinement] when the door is large, whereas for a bird, it becomes a renunciant (*yati*) only when it has actually exited through a small door. Thus, he would become a "twice-born" (renunciant) in heart.
And in this verse, four positions are specified:
the position of binding the ankles,
and the position of placing the feet within the cage at the great gate.
The cage is at the narrow entrance;
when both are removed, it is the point of conjunction.
"From a place," and so forth:
a certain ascetic goes from this place to another place,
or he carries a message for someone.

In that regard, if one should transfer that entrusted wealth or property from one limb to another limb or to the head with a thieving mind, he incurs a breach of the vow and the ascetic practice (*dhuta*);
the meaning is that he becomes a non-practitioner (*ayati*).
Thus, by this verse, the locations of the limbs of the body have been stated.
"He has died," and so forth: when a mendicant, having heard from another traveler— that is,

from a fellow celibate student (*brahmacārin*)— that a certain person for whom a specific object was entrusted has died, and yet, failing to give a share to one who is habituated to staying at the boundary of the monastery, takes that object for himself, he becomes neither a true ascetic nor a non-ascetic [he falls into a state of transgression].
"He becomes one who is no longer a śrāmaṇera," and so forth;
here too, the "place" refers specifically to a part of the body.
Now, regarding the question of to whom the property of a deceased novice (śrāmaṇera) belongs, he says:
"Whatever wealth," and so forth.
The Sage spoke thus: "Whatever property belongs to a deceased ascetic (yati) or an Arhat who has attained final nirvāṇa, all that goes to the preceptor (upādhyāya).
This means the Blessed One said: "To the one who takes it," and so forth.
These elephants roam in a vast area;
however, some ascetic might capture an elephant there.
If the elephant were to go toward the direction desired and intended by that captor, [the merit would accrue to him].
When that elephant had gone in the direction intended by its captor and leader, the practitioner remained true to his vow; meanwhile, the *karipa*—
one who protects (*pāti*) the elephant (*kariṇam*)— that is, the elephant-keeper, [acted].
In that sacrificial fire;
of what kind?
One from which consciousness has been removed.

When there is one who possesses the perception "the elephant has been taken by me"—that is, when the perceiver of the taking exists—then that taker, though observing the vow, would become a thief and cease to be a *śramaṇa*.
By this verse, the four quarters [of the argument] are established;
it is the undesired position (*anabhimatā dik*).
The four points taught are: the preparatory stage, and the obstructing mind.
"Offering-robe," and so forth:
a robe and garland for the purpose of offering is an "offering-robe-garland"; its two ends—
Its release is liberation, which is the removal [of attachment];
by means of that, having abandoned the two extremes, when there is a falling or a dropping upon the ground— that is, on the earth— then one falls away from the garland of robes.
Why? Because of restraint (*saṃvara*);
the word "restraint" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
Even by taking a silken garment from the Bodhi tree, one becomes an ascetic (*ayati*).
By this verse, three points are established:
bondage at both extremes, and the appropriation of others by means of the mind.
And regarding "clothing":
in that context, when a series of robes is fastened to a peg, the location is the two ends.
When both persons, through mutual ignorance, steal [the robes] by releasing the two ends of the series of robes, then the location is their mutual possession.
But in the case of tearing or cutting it, that very garment is the place [of the offense].
"Cast off," and so forth.

That great family in which pearl necklaces and other such items have been cast away or scattered is described as such. When a mendicant has gone there and a companion has arisen, he takes the pearl necklaces and other items scattered from that family and places them in the hand or the pouch of that very companion. If that [mendicant] causes those items to be lost by that very companion, will it be said that there is a lapse in his restraint (*saṃvara*)?
"By one with matted hair," and so forth.

Alternatively, by a shaggy dog—that is, a *kurkura*—causing that pearl necklace or the like to be taken away from that noble family; or by taking away a calf, such as a young cow-calf, with grass and the like—is there a falling away from the vow (*saṃvara*)?
How much more so [in the case of humans]? (SŚ 32)
Does the abandonment of the vow (*saṃvara*) occur merely by stepping down from one’s feet? No, he says.
"If the conventional behavior (*upacāra*) is abandoned by them, there is a lapse of the vow.
If that conventional behavior—like that of dogs—is abandoned by them, [then the vow is lost].
At that time, the ascetic abandons his restraint;
and here, the transgression of conventional conduct consists in the transgression of seeing and hearing.
"At night," and so forth:
a certain ascetic binds cows, carts, horses, and the like during the night, thinking, "These [beings] will carry these [loads]. In this case, one should prescribe [the penance] as before.
That is to say, "one becomes one whose restraint has lapsed.

Thus, by means of these three verses beginning with that, it is stated by way of metaphor that the mind [resides] in carts and so forth, as well as its designation as such and the acquisition of the sense of "mine" regarding them.
"Upright," and so forth.
Suppose a certain ascetic steals a necklace; in that case, if there is a straight peg [to hang it upon],...
And when the binding is firm, then as it is being lifted, the binding releases its place on the peg; thus it is said that it has been displaced from its position without further attachment.
Furthermore, in the act of lifting, there would be a thief.
Now, even if the peg becomes crooked and the binding becomes loose,
one does not yet cease to be a *śrāmaṇera*.
By means of the crookedness of the peg and the looseness of the binding, he demonstrates that the peg does not overstep its place.
And because he has been moved from a state that is free of consequences, he is not a non-śrāmaṇera;
however, when he is released from all bonds in every respect, then he becomes a non-yati.
"Having pierced," and so forth: having made a hole in a jar, [one places] ghee (sarpiḥ), honey (kṣaudram), and so on.
If a mendicant takes oil, such as sesame oil,
or water, such as that from a river, and if he should cross a flood or if the stream should break, then he incurs a disturbance of his vows (*saṃvara*).
The meaning is that it becomes extended.
However, if within an uninterrupted stream [of practice] one turns back with regard to the state of a recluse (*śrāmaṇya*), then it does not become so; thus explain those who know the Vinaya.
"Vaṇṭayamāṇa," and so forth:
when the property of two brothers is being divided in their home,
*lipsā* is the desire to obtain, the longing for gain.
If, out of that desire for gain, one should take even as much land as a mere child could span from the share of a brother, then one becomes one whose vow is broken;
thus, in this context, the basis of intention has been explained.
Now, furthermore, if a bowl or similar item has been seized by thieves, may it be taken back slowly by one who has abandoned the intent [of theft]?
"No," he says, and so forth with the words "by a thief" and so on.
If a mendicant, having become despondent regarding a bowl or other items taken—that is, seized—by a thief or robber, should take them up again, he falls away from his restraint (*saṃvara*).
*Saṃvara* is the act of restraining (*saṃvaraṇa*).
It is an obstruction to the flow of unwholesome states;
from that, one is diminished.
But the other, whose intention is not manifest, does not incur misfortune when taking them up again.
The meaning is that there is no future existence.
Furthermore, is it permissible to take back those bowls and other items seized by thieves that were given by cowherds and others? To this he says:
"A friend," and so forth.

If that bowl taken by thieves should be obtained through friendship, or given with great generosity, or offered by cowherds and others, then for the mendicant taking it, no offense is recognized; the meaning is that even a minor transgression (duṣkṛta) does not occur.
If thieves take the bowl and robes and do not give them back, one asks how one should act;
he says: "In fear," and so forth.
For the sake of liberating one's bowl and robes, one should display fear of those thieves;
however, one must not go to the king where the imprisonment and so forth of those bandits occurs and say, "We have been robbed by these thieves."
"Niṣkāsayasi" and so forth:
these two ascetics, while making a formal agreement (*kriyākāra*), cause each other to perform the *prayāja* sacrifice.
Whatever bowl and robes belong to the preceptors (*upādhyāya*) and teachers (*ācārya*), you are removing that which belongs to both of us—to you and to me.
Having spoken thus, "that," if even a single ascetic should steal that bowl and robe, then both of those practitioners become thieves.
[The phrase] "one's own property," and so forth, [follows].
When these two ascetics steal their own property with a thieving mind,

in that case, by one half-share of one ascetic, even that [first] ascetic becomes a non-ascetic; and by the other half-share expelled by the other person, the second [ascetic] also becomes a non-ascetic.
Now, if many śrāmaṇeras were to conspire and steal five māṣakas minus one kārṣāpaṇa, would they then be considered restrained (*saṃvarin*) or not?
They are indeed unrestrained (*asaṃvarin*), because they share a single intention,
like several novices standing at a single door.
"We shall give," and so forth.
These ascetics, being of one mind, made a formal agreement with the elder:
"Elder, we shall give you an equal share."
"Stay only at the gate; we shall commit the theft.
Having made such a promise to him, he carries out what was said; thus, he is called "one who does what was said" (*uktakṛt*).
The offense for that elder who has done as instructed is equal [to that of the others]. With whom is it equal? He says:
with the novice thieves.
The meaning is that she, too, would become a thief.
"Having stayed," and so forth:
a certain visiting ascetic, having stayed— that is,
having made his dwelling— and having forgotten his bowl and robes, departs.
When that guest has departed, whichever monk comes again and again and causes his bowl and robes to be taken away becomes a thief.
This applies to all resident monks and so forth.
