By means of this aforementioned practice, if all the resident monks were to take away the bowl of a guest, then they would all have their vows impaired.
But he to whom that bowl and robe belong— if he leads them away having remembered [the owner]— is not guilty;
"guilty" (kilviṣin) refers to one who has committed a transgression (pāpa).
"Because he has that, he is 'one with defilement' (kilviṣaḥ)"; [the phrase] "not one with defilement" means that he would be without offense.
"Of another," and so forth.
If a novice monk, with a thieving mind, causes another ascetic to bring a bowl for him by means of yet another ascetic, he becomes guilty of an offense;
the meaning is that he ceases to be an ascetic.
If one who brings you has such an understanding—that "this is the vessel for this very person who brought me"—then there is no fault;
this person does not partake in the fault because of the absence of a thieving mind.
However, those who read, "the ascetic who brings [the food] along is the one observing the vow," [hold a different view].
Since the meaning of "together" (*saha*) is already expressed by the third case (*tṛtīyā*) even without the word *saha*, the inclusion of the word *saha* is redundant;
or rather, this third case does not have the sense of "together," because it is prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*).
Because of the correlative relationship between *yat* and *tat*, the use of the word *tat* is omitted;
therefore, the reading should be "yaḥ anīya-yati-vratī" (he who is a self-controlled ascetic observing vows),
followed by "yāvat pūjā" and so forth.

Thinking that as long as worship is performed for the Sage, the Buddha, the Blessed One, so long will worship and honor continue for the Saṅgha as well, one who—with a mind of theft—gives property belonging to the Saṅgha to a stūpa, or property belonging to a stūpa to the Saṅgha, has his vows broken; the meaning is that he becomes a non-recluse (*ayati*).
Now, is it not the case that whatever prosperities there may be, they all come from having relied upon the Blessed One?
It is not the case that through proper mental attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) there is no possibility of a thieving mind arising;
for it is precisely this [proper attention] that incites the thieving mind, just as compassion incites one to carry away water.
How could taking what is not given be established for him?
Furthermore, is it permissible to take funds set aside for the repair of a stūpa from the treasury belonging to the Saṅgha? He said:
"No," and so forth, as detailed in the full text.
Whether by those serving for a day, for a fortnight, or for a month, one should take a withdrawal from the communal treasury after recording it;
[this applies] mutually among one another,
and [funds] may be taken from the stupa for the sake of the Saṃgha.
The meaning is: "from the Saṃgha and from the stūpa.

And by those stewards, upon the completion of the undertaking of the work, it must be stated: "This much gold, silver, and so forth was taken from the stūpa's property, and this much from the property of the Saṃgha.
It is not otherwise for one who has performed what was prescribed.
How otherwise?
If they were to take up a loan without having it written down, and did not mention it at the end of the month, [how could there be a dispute?]
Then they are "not-doers of what was said.
They are called "not-doers of what was said" because they do not carry out what was told;
the meaning is that they incur a transgression (duṣkṛta).
"Own part" (*svāṃśa*), and so forth.
In this context, "part" (*aṃśa*), "portion" (*bhāga*), and "member" (*avayava*) are synonymous. One's own part is a "own-part" (*svāṃśa*).

One who takes away that portion belonging to another which has been relinquished by him is called a "taker of what was relinquished" (*svāṃśamuktahara*), meaning one who takes a share apart from his own allotted portion.
These two types of ascetics obtain gains within a single family.
Between those two, the novice monk who takes the superior portion becomes a thief.
However, one who takes it with the thought, "I shall restore the trust," does not incur guilt.
[As for the phrase] "Do you receive it? and so forth...
These two ascetics make a formal agreement (*kriyākāra*):

"Whatever gain you obtain and whatever gain I obtain, that shall belong to both of us, you and me. Having made this agreement, when a gain arises, whoever violates that agreement becomes a thief by reason of taking half of it.
The meaning is that by a portion of the second type of ascetic, one becomes a non-śrāmaṇera.
"Regarding the instruction on the gift as well, it is thus," and so forth.

Just as it was stated that there is a falling away from the restraint for one who breaks a formal agreement between two families under protection, the same should be understood regarding the instruction on the gift.

The assignment of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists in the recitation of verses on giving. Furthermore, when two practitioners of the rag-robe tradition (*pāṃśukūlika*) have both obtained rag-robes, he who violates the formal agreement (*kriyākāra*) becomes one whose vows are lost (*cyutasaṃvara*).
It was previously stated that the gain belonging to the Saṃgha must not be given to a stūpa, nor that which belongs to a stūpa to the Saṃgha.
To demonstrate the rule— showing that it is even more impossible to give it to anyone else—
he says "one who is helpful," and so forth, for the purpose of abandoning the misconception [that such giving is permissible].
Those whose nature is to assist are benefactors; by contrast, those who do not assist are non-benefactors.
To them, food, drink, and so forth belonging to the Saṅgha should be given.
Who, then, are these? He says:
the benefactors, such as the king and others who are the owners of the monastery, and the non-benefactors, such as thieves and others; both of these should be understood respectively.
"Even from those who are wealthy," and so forth.
If novices perform tasks such as plastering or sweeping in a monastery belonging to the Saṃgha, then they should be given a morning meal and so on by the Saṃgha; otherwise, they should not.
By the word "even" (*api*), it is shown that not only those who have helped or harmed [the community] are to be understood, but also those who perform such services for the wealthy.

But surely, since a novice (śrāmaṇera) has already gone forth, he is indeed permitted to enjoy the food and drink belonging to the Saṅgha even without performing tasks such as plastering the monastery;

for what purpose, then, is it said "even from those who are wealthy"? Anticipating this very objection, [the author] states that in the Sūtra, the Blessed One permitted a monk who is adorned with the three robes to enjoy the food and drink belonging to the Saṅgha.

Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of no obstacle whatsoever for a śramaṇa, saying: "Even from those who are densely endowed with glory. Nor should one apply speculative reasoning to the Vinaya, thinking, "This is merely something trivial."
Regarding the passage beginning with "sīmāntasthāyinaḥ":

to that ascetic who has the habit of staying within the boundary (sīmā), who is accompanied by monks, and who performs the service of attending upon the monks—having given him rice and so forth under the pretext of a child’s bowl, the ascetic should take the rice and such;
some, however, read the word "na" at the end, [meaning] he should not take the rice and so forth.

The meaning here is that one should not take rice and so forth under the pretext of being for a child without having given it to the ascetic who stands at the boundary; considering the suffix *-tāti* as being elided (*praśliṣṭa*), he explains it thus. Thus, there is no fault in either of these two readings: "without giving to one who stays at the boundary" or "to the ascetic who falls within the boundary."
"Without having abandoned hope," and so forth:
he by whom hope for [receiving] a bowl and other requisites has not been abandoned is described as such.
[He thinks], "My own bowl and robe have been lost."
It was not taken away by anyone, but was somehow dropped through negligence;
seeing it, one should give rise to the thought, "I shall take it," and thus take it.
How is it that one should think thus?
Thinking that one who has not abandoned desire may take back a lost bowl or robe, but not another;
the author asks what kind of ascetic such a greedy person is, and answers: "one whose bowl and so forth have been lost."
One whose bowls and other requisites have been lost is described in this way:
"One should not abandon hope at all," meaning,
"I shall surely recover the lost bowl and so forth right where it was."
The meaning is that one should be wise in such a way as to think, "I shall take it right there.
However, for one who, having become free from expectation, takes up a bowl or robe that has been lost, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no relinquishing of the vow,
for by that [act] he has not committed a secondary theft against the thief, since the property was not actually stolen.

In order to show that there is an offense of wrongdoing (*duṣkṛta*) even when one transgresses the formal agreement regarding the preliminary acts and so forth— by way of the consequence of making such an agreement for the sake of gain— he says:
"Recitation," and so forth.
These novices, having established a communal agreement (*saṃghaśīlaka*), make a formal resolution (*kriyākāra*):
"We shall perform recitation, study, or instruction. Having made such a resolution, those who do not abide by that resolution—

"They are transgressors of what is spoken by the Jina": those whose habit is to transgress the discipline (*vinaya*) which was spoken (*udita*)—that is, declared (*ukta*)—by the Jina, the Blessed Buddha, are "transgressors of what is spoken by the Jina";
the meaning is that they incur a misdeed (*duṣkṛta*).
Thus, by this, it is explained that in every such case, there is an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta) when one transgresses a formal agreement concerning a righteous act.
Regarding the passage beginning with "patākā" (banner):
an ascetic should not take from a stūpa items characterized as flags, banners, and so forth.
Furthermore, the mention of the "stūpa of the Nirgrantha" is intended as an illustrative example.
Therefore, even for one who takes [an object] from a stūpa of the Paṇḍara-bhikṣu and the like, there would indeed be a *duṣkṛta* offense,

but not a loss of the vow (*saṃvaratyāga*), because there is no owner. However, in the case of a stūpa where a *devalaka* (temple attendant) resides, for one who takes [an object] from it, there would certainly be a loss of the vow.
However, that which is raised up, shaken, or cast down by the wind—that is, flags and so forth—should be understood as "dust" and thus grasped [as such].
Regarding the phrase "the duty of toll" (*śulkakṛtyam*) and so forth:
by the word *śulka*, the place where revenue is generated for the royal household is meant;
it is what common people refer to as a *ghaṭṭa*.
In this context, "purpose" refers to the motive;
however, for the sake of taking another's property from that place in order to withhold appropriate gifts, a monk should neither take that property himself nor cause it to be taken by another.
Regarding the payment of a toll, one should not teach the means for its avoidance, such as: "Go by this path,
and then you will not have to pay the toll," or "By giving a jewel," and so forth.
It is also said that a certain merchant of deceitful character, in order to escape paying customs duties, gave jewels to ascetics before the customs checkpoint at an increased rate;
subsequently, by means of a fraudulent arrangement involving the customs officials and the ascetics, he sought to recover those jewels.
It must be understood that the ascetics were unaware of his intention beforehand.
Otherwise, there would be a loss of restraint.

If that [nature] were not fully understood by those ascetics, they would reprimand him thoroughly, saying, "O deluded man, you are indeed deceiving us! and then that jewel should be returned to that very merchant.
"There is no fee," and so forth.
There is no fee for the Sage, the Blessed Buddha.
Those who possess vows are "vow-holders" (vratinaḥ).

This is "for use" (pāribhogika) because it is for the purpose of enjoyment; regarding such an object for use, there is no fee (śulka) for those observing vows, just as there is none for a Sage (muni). It is implied that a fee exists in other cases.
Therefore, he says:
"The one who performs buying and selling shall give.
One who performs buying and selling is a "buyer-seller-maker" (krayavikrayakṛt); such a renunciant (yati) must pay the toll.
Regarding the phrase "the one who has entered the rains-retreat" and so forth:
in whichever village or town a novice (śrāmaṇera) has entered the rains-retreat, the gains belonging to the rains-retreat (varṣāvāsika-lābha) must be given to him there.
The gains of the rainy-season residence (*varṣāvāsika-lābha*) must also be given to those two novices for whom there has been a loss of both life and the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

By this it is meant: except for those who are terrified by the fear of obstacles to life or terrified by the fear of obstacles to the holy life, the gains of the rainy-season residence should not be given to others who have not spent the rains.
[This applies to] those who have previously entered [the retreat], and so forth.

Those novice monks (*śrāmaṇera*) who have entered the rains retreat on the first day of the month of Śrāvaṇa must request the rain-retreat dwelling (*varṣāvāsika*) starting from the first day of the month of Āśvina.
However, those who have entered the rains retreat later, on the first day of the month of Bhādrapada, must do so later, in the month of Kārttika.
If everyone enters on the first day, then by the authority of the Saṃgha, even those who entered later must request the rain-retreat dwelling simultaneously with the others.
"Again he grasps," and so forth.
In that context, "the thing" (vastu) refers to the state of being a complete object;
"the utterance of speech" (vāk-pravyāhāra) is that which illuminates a specific meaning.
Taking "karma" to mean "action" (kriyā),
or [deriving it] from the sense that "by this [it] is performed," the word *karma* here specifically denotes the ritual act of full ordination (*upasaṃpad-karman*).
By that very action, that person is made a monk.
"Vastu-karman" refers to both the object and the action;
"jugupsā" is the revulsion toward or censure of those two.

According to that [view], even for a person who, having abandoned the status of a monk, takes up initiation and renunciation once again, an equal share of gains must be given along with those who have completed the rains-retreat;
however, others explain it differently.
From the request for the three refuges up to the donning of the saffron robes—this is the *vastu* (matter);

"I follow the Buddha, the Blessed One, who has gone forth, into the homeless life"—this is the *karma* (action). Because it illuminates a distinguished meaning, it is considered the *kriyākarma* (action of performance).
Both the *vastu* and the *karma* together constitute the *vastukarma* (matter-and-action).
Disgust for those two means censure;

even for that person who, having abandoned the status of a śrāmaṇera, takes up initiation and the life of a renunciant once again, an equal share of gains must be given along with the ascetics who have resided there for a year.
To the question "Who says this?", he replies: "The All-Knowing One";
that is to say, the Blessed One said it.

"Having spent the rains," and so forth. In this context, "having spent the rains" means not having remained [in retreat] for the three months. "Confused" refers to one who has left the state of renunciation after having gone forth.
One whose view is contemptible is a "wrong-viewer" (*kudṛṣṭi*);
this means one who possesses false views (*mithyādṛṣṭika*). And false view is the activity of a nihilist—[thinking], "There is no mother," and so forth.
There is no father;
there is no ripening of the fruit of well-done or ill-done deeds.
Upon the cessation of the life-faculty, one is dead.
One who has gone to another country, and one who has gone elsewhere from that place;
these five persons do not deserve a share.
"‘It should be given to such-and-such,’ and so forth:

when a gain has arisen [with the thought], ‘This gain of mine must be given to such-and-such a monk,’ if at that time some ascetic should die, then the Blessed One has declared that this gain must certainly and inevitably be given to that designated monk."
"Going to another region," and so forth:

when a monk has stayed in this region for three months and then goes to another region, whatever gain he obtains should be deposited in a ritual hall (*kalpa*) or a ritual hut (*kalpakuṭī*). And when three types of persons—those who have not spent the rains retreat, those who are distracted, and those with wrong views—bring harm to the Saṃgha, [the deposit is to be used].
In that case, the wise should not give food, drink, or other requisites belonging to the Saṅgha to them after they have consumed [the meal].
But has it not been stated that "the group of five does not deserve a share"?
For what purpose, then, are these two verses beginning with "it should be given to such-and-such" being spoken?
This is true;
however, when one dies without conceptual construction and departs before any attainment has arisen, [one proceeds to the state of non-conceptualization].

Furthermore, when three types of persons—those who have not lived the rains retreat, those who are distracted, and those with wrong views—perform an act that is purposeless, these five persons do not deserve the gain;
conversely, they do deserve it in the opposite case. Thus, there is no fault, as this allows for the possibility of exceptions.
"Garments," and so forth: these ascetics have entered the rainy season retreat within a family.
In that case, if the donor should speak in general terms, saying, "I shall give garments," [the rule applies].

The gain that arises through these four expressions— "I will give a robe," "I will give the price for a robe," "I will give the price for a covering"— is obtained by those who are present face-to-face, and not by others.
"Varṣāvāsika," and so forth; "I shall give clothing for those who have completed the rainy-season retreat," namely, a robe.
Whatever gain arises from these four terms— namely, "purchase of coverings" and "purchase of robes"— accrues to those who have spent the rainy season retreat.
If a donor gives the gains belonging to that rainy-season residence even to those who did not reside during the rains,
then there is no fault for those who accept it according to the donor's wish.
Regarding the passage beginning with "yāmika" and so forth:

on whichever day the Blessed One was born and on which day he attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the great festival and worship held on those occasions constitute the festivals of birth, enlightenment, and so forth.
The gain that arises from that is thus described as follows:
"requisites for the deceased" (*mṛtapariṣkāra*) and "minor requisites" (*kṣudrapariṣkāra*), etc., forming a *dvandva* compound;

[furthermore], there are those that are for a specific time (*kālika*), for a watch of the night (*yāmika*), for as long as life lasts (*yāvajjīvika*), for seven days (*sāptāhika*), requisites for the deceased, minor requisites, and daily requisites (*naityaka*).
The tenfold gain— consisting of out-of-season robes, the construction of a hut, and the great occurrences such as birth and enlightenment— is obtained by those who are present.
"Non-appropriable," and so forth:
that which is the bedding and seating belonging to the Saṅgha is "non-appropriable";
the meaning is that it must not be given away because it constitutes an obstruction [to the community].
It must not be sold,
nor should it be consumed by making it into a *paudgalika* (private) possession.
As for those who are *śrāmaṇeras*:
If they give away communal bedding and seating as a personal possession, sell it, or use it for private purposes, they commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
"Regarding 'to the Saṅgha of the four directions' and so forth:
a certain donor, possessing some material substance,
at some time gives it to the noble Saṅgha of the four directions."
Whether it be for the Buddha, the Blessed One, or for the Saṅgha present before him, the ascetic should offer all that [gift] accordingly;
and what has been given to the four quarters of the world must be offered specifically to those of the four quarters— this is the general principle.
"Having given silently," and so forth:
suppose some donor, having come to a monastery and given pearls and other such gifts, should depart in silence.
When that donor has departed after giving silently, the pearls and other items must be offered to the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Whatever bedding and seating there may be, that should be given to the Saṃgha of the four directions;
however, clothing and such items should be given to the Saṃgha that is present before one.
"With how many factors (*aṅga*) is one endowed when taking what has not been given that one ceases to be a śramaṇera? He replied:
"A large object," and so forth.
"Large" means extensive.
What is that substance?
It is five *māṣakas* less one *kākinī*.
He says that this may even sometimes be one's own property.
Regarding the phrase "appropriated by another":
since it may happen that even when a substance is appropriated by another, a mendicant does not have the perception of it as being so appropriated, he says:
"one who has that perception" means one who has the perception of it as being appropriated by another.
Sometimes all of this may occur, yet there is no intention to steal; therefore, the phrase "intention to steal" is used. Furthermore, the meaning is that a mind of theft must be present.
One might think that even if these four factors were present, the substance [of the vow] might not fall away from its place; therefore, he says:
"and falling from one's place.
A mendicant endowed with five factors does not lose his restraint (*saṃvara*), even if he takes what has not been given.
He asks, "By which five? and replies,
"One who has the notion of 'given,' the notion of 'one's own,' and the notion of 'not appropriated by another'— such is the ascetic as described."
Moreover, even one who takes [something] from his own portion and for a limited time does not lose his vow (*saṃvara*).
Regarding the phrase "having taken what was not given," etc.:
"having taken" means having seized.

Furthermore, the "stolen object" (adattaṃ dravyaṃ), having leaped up and gone to the sky— the firmament— reaches the four directions; that is to say, the four cardinal points, since the word *āśā* is a synonym for *dik* (direction).
"In that very place" means:
because he has returned and sat down there once again,
his restraint becomes impaired.
The meaning is that he becomes a wanderer (*yati*).
"One who has been purchased, etc. is the detailed explanation: a certain wanderer may be purchased by someone.
Or, if that hired laborer takes another's property out of ignorance, through a lapse of memory, or with the notion that it is his own, his vow is impaired.
However, ascetics whose minds are deranged or distracted do not incur an offense even when taking the property of others, because they lack the intention to steal.

In this context, the abandonment of the vow (*saṃvaratyāga*) is explained by the series of statements beginning with "therein, [the vow is] occasional" (*kālika*) and ending with "it is the same even regarding the instruction on the sacrificial fee" (*dakṣiṇādeśana*).
The misdeeds (*duṣkṛta*) are illustrated by the series of statements beginning with "toward those who have helped or harmed" and ending with "having given [the gift] silently.
By the remaining [statements], the fivefold restriction (*pāñcāṅganiyama*) is established.
If an ascetic, with the intent to steal, carries a heavy object contained in a vessel for eleven yojanas, he either becomes Śrīghana [the deity of wealth] or does not.
In the *Sphuṭārthā*, the commentary on the *Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha*, this is the second precept: abstaining from taking what is not given.
Having obtained the opportunity characterized by the training rule of abstaining from sexual intercourse, he speaks with reference to that [opportunity],
beginning with "man, woman," and so forth.
Man, woman, and eunuch— these are "men, women, and eunuchs"— and their excrement, urine, and mouths are as follows:

If a novice monk, having inserted even a sesame-seed-sized portion of his male organ into whatever opening, fissure, or cavity of theirs, should experience the taste [of pleasure], he becomes one whose vows are broken;
the meaning is that he falls from his restraint.
Showing that one who engages in sexual intercourse even with those who are not of the human realm—namely, women, men, and eunuchs—incurs the loss of restraint (*saṃvara*), he says:
"But they [are] human and non-human," and so forth. Regarding this, there is a dispute concerning the reading of the verse (*kārikā*).
In this regard, some, reading the text as "those [beings] are human and non-human, as well as animals, humans, and so forth," explain it as follows:
He says, "humans and so forth"— by the word "and so forth," women and eunuchs are included.
"By that, 'men and so forth' means men, women, and eunuchs; those included within the human realm."

It should be understood that those included in the realm of non-humans and those included in the animal realm—men, women, and eunuchs—are based on sexual intercourse whether they are awake, dead, or asleep.
Others, however, reading the text as "those who are human and non-human, and those animals such as the *amara*s," speak thus: "Those who are human and non-human... [and so forth].

By the word "that" (tat), the men, women, and eunuchs mentioned immediately prior are included, because the word "that" refers to what has been stated most recently. The particle "tu" (but) has the sense of the restrictive particle "eva" (only).
Only those men, women, and eunuchs—whether belonging to the human realm, the non-human realm, or the animal realm—are, when awake, dead, or asleep, each individually based upon sexual intercourse.
These are to be understood as follows:
"Amarādayaḥ" means the immortals, i.e., the gods; by the word "ādi" (and so forth), other destinies are also included.

Therefore, even among those comprised within the destinies of gods, asuras, hell-beings, and pretas—whether they be women, men, or eunuchs—one who engages in sexual intercourse abandons their restraint (*saṃvara*).
However, this [interpretation] alone is logical.

For otherwise, since the inclusion of humans, women, and others would already be established by the phrase "humans and so forth" (*narādayaḥ*), the inclusion of the word *tat* ("those") would be redundant.
Furthermore, if it is thought that "by the word *tat*, those very same humans and non-humans are connected [to the following]," this is incoherent.
For when words are directly perceived, the word *tat* (that) is not employed by the wise, as that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Nor can it be said that the word *tat* refers to the connection with the apertures of the mouth, anus, and urinary tract,
because the word *randhra* (aperture) is neuter in gender and is used here in the singular number.

And here, because of the reference using the masculine gender and the plural number in the phrase "these [beings] of yours," if it is thought that we shall explain them as "the specific openings of the anus, the urinary tract, and the mouth"— just as the specific openings of the anus, the urinary tract, and the mouth [distinguish] women, men, and eunuchs, and are comprised within the destinies of humans, non-humans, and animals— then [it follows that...]

"They are to be known as based on sexual intercourse"—this is an unprecedented connection between the action and its agent. This is because there is no genitive of relation (saṃbandha-ṣaṣṭhī) such as "of men" (*narādīnām*), and because another interpretation is adopted. Therefore, the reading should be *amarādaya* [not *narādaya*].

When this has been thus considered, some say: "In the reading *narādayaḥ* (humans and so forth), by the word *ādi* (and so forth), there will be the inclusion of women, eunuchs, and other modes of movement (*gati*);
what contradiction is there in this?"

In this context, not all animal births (*tiryagyoni*) are intended, because some, being subtle or gross, are incapable of sexual union; rather, it is shown that only specific ones are meant. Thus he says: "beginning with the female elephant," and so forth.
From the species of female elephants up to the species of chickens—

in this interval, whichever species is relatively smaller or larger in comparison to another, by going toward each such species and engaging in sexual intercourse within that particular species, one falls from the vow;
the meaning is that one ceases to be a *śrāmaṇera*.

Precisely because of this initial specification, for one who errs regarding a species that is larger than the species of female elephants, or a species that is smaller than the species of chickens, there is no forfeiture of the vow.
But it would be a misdeed.

Demonstrating that an ascetic (*yati*) does not tolerate merely engaging in sexual intercourse, but does not tolerate even the sight of a woman and so forth, he says: "Being impassioned," and so on in detail.
An ascetic, being fully impassioned, should not look upon a woman.
And he should not hear her voice;
being himself unclothed, he should not approach nor go toward an unclothed woman.
And one should not discharge the male organ;
because of performing [the act] here according to this rule, there is an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta) in every case.
Furthermore, does one who engages in sexual intercourse even with a [female body] that has been split lose his restraint (*saṃvara*)?
He says: "It does," beginning with the words "by two walls" and so forth.

A novice (*śrāmaṇera*) who—having taken apart the vulva (*koṭarikā*), which is designated as the locus of the female organ, having dried it with wind, sun, or the like, or having cut it into separate pieces with a weapon, and having moistened it with sesame oil and such, and then having joined and unified them—[engages in intercourse].
If she acts perversely, she should be expelled;
provided that there is a formal assembly, if that *koṭarikā* joins the assembly.
Then there is a fault, but not at other times.
"Below, above," and so forth:
suppose a certain woman were cut into three pieces;
one would not pass through her lower section nor her upper section, because of the discoloration, bloating, and putrefaction.
Furthermore, one should not even go near a skeleton that is smeared with pus, blood, and so forth; this is the detailed meaning of the phrase "a white skeleton.
A "white skeleton" refers to a skeleton that is pale or white.

One should not approach a woman made of stone set upon a rock, one made of wood, one made of clay, one fashioned from plaster, or even one made of cloth, so long as she is merely a skeleton of white bones.
A pair (*mithuna*) is a couple consisting of a woman and a man; the particular pleasure that arises therein is *maithuna* (sexual intercourse).
Therefore, "one who is always—i.e., at all times—restrained from it" is an epithet of the ascetic (*yati*).
"Having gone into meditation," and so forth. "Gone" means attained.

One who has gone into meditative absorption and sleep is one who has entered a state of dhyāna and is overcome by drowsiness; likewise, one who is awakened yet remains as if sleeping due to the effects of drinking liquor and the like.

Or, when the mind of a practitioner is distracted by intoxication, imbalance of the great elements, and so forth, or pierced and pained by harsh sensation, and some woman, having seized him by force, inserts her own organ into the practitioner’s organ—if that woman sits down upon him by force, what [offense] is there? He says: [it is an offense].

"At the beginning, middle," and so forth: one should bring to completion the aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) that occurs at the beginning, at the time of entering the limbs of the drama, as well as in the middle and at the conclusion.
What is the ascetic like?
He has not yet emerged from that meditative absorption;
he must be roused from his dwelling.
"But in the absence of relishing, it is not [so].
It should be understood that this was said with reference to a person who possesses strong, middling, or weak passion.
Regarding what was stated—that one should relish at the beginning, middle, and end—it is asked: "What is this so-called 'relishing'? He says:
"Various," and so forth: the enjoyment of rice-gruel endowed with various kinds of condiments and flavors—that is, being provided with them—should be understood as analogous to that [experience].
Just as the tasting and drinking of clear food-liquor or *surā* wine by a drunkard or a madman is like oil, in the same way, the tasting of sexual intercourse is to be understood.
Others explain it differently: "śauṇḍa" means that which exists in *śuṇḍi*s.
What, then, is this? It is grain-liquor (*annāsava*). Of what kind is it? It is clear as oil (*tailāccha*).
Just as with oil, that which is clear and intoxicating is a grain-based liquor (*annāsava*);
its drinking is its consumption. What is it like? It should be understood as a tasting.
Furthermore, as to what "lack of relish" (anāsvāda) is like, he says: "The neck of a youth," and so forth. It is, for example, like the binding of a dead dog around the neck of a young man.
And just as the touch of glowing iron would be for a delicate man, so should that taste be understood.
It is called *dhyāna* because one meditates by means of it.
The meaning is that they perceive it;
and that [perception] becomes fourfold due to the distinction of its constituent parts (aṅga),
by way of the divisions of the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
It is established that "sleep" has the meaning of a contraction of the mind that is incapable of sustaining the body; these two are "meditative absorption and sleep."
"Avakrīta," and so forth;
its meaning is to be understood according to the preceding rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).
"Passion-demon," and so forth.
Passion (*rāga*) is that which colors; or, it is called passion because by means of it the mind is colored.
One should never touch that part of the body which has been activated by passion and the like for the purpose of discharging semen.
To the question "With what [should one not touch it]? he replies:
"With the elements such as earth and so forth."
"By engaging in horizontal union," and so forth:

because one observes the practice of horizontal sexual intercourse, and because of the sight of men and women acting out of negligence, if an emission of semen should occur due to intense passion and the like, then the ascetic should reproach his mind, thinking: "A deformed act has been committed by me; I shall not do so again."
"From marrow," and so forth: that which is produced from marrow is "marrow-born," namely semen; its "flowing" is its emission.
If a practitioner emits semen even in a dream,
no fault occurs for him. To explain how this is so, he says:
He states the reason:
"In a dream," and so forth.
Five types of dreams are mentioned in the Vinaya.
Just as a true dream was seen by the Bodhisattva,
and just as a false dream was seen, so it is not the case that the false is unreal;
[rather,] there is the "unpracticed dream," which is when an object that ought to be constantly performed is seen.

The "endless dream" (*anantasvapna*) is that which is seen throughout the entire night and cannot be delimited; the "dream within a dream" (*svapnasvapna*) is when one dream is seen within another dream.
This is what is meant: when a practitioner experiences the emission of semen in a dream, [it is a dream within a dream].
Not even the slightest fault accrues to him because the dream is unreal;
otherwise, the holy life would be insecure, since there would be the consequence of incurring an offense through engaging in sexual intercourse even in a dream.

"By passion," and so forth: with a mind that is "possessed"—that is, seized—by passion, Śrīghana should not touch a woman (nārī), meaning a female; nor a man or a eunuch (puṃnapuṃsakam), which means a male or a hermaphrodite.
The remainder is easy to understand.

Regarding "breasts, armpits," and so forth: it is a *dvandva* compound consisting of breasts (*stanau*), armpits (*kakṣe*), lips (*oṣṭhau*), navel (*nābhi*), thighs (*ūrū*), sides (*pārśve*), belly (*kukṣi*), and the movement of excrement (*malabhrama*).
Therefore, being impassioned, the ascetic should not revile—that is, he should not utter censure of—those delusions concerning the breasts, armpits, lips, navel, thighs, sides, and belly;
nor should he praise them, that is, he should not extol them. This is the meaning.
"Your breasts are either unattractive or attractive, as is your body hair"—to which [the opponent] asks, "Of whom are those breasts, armpits, and so forth? he replies:
"Of women."
Here, by the term "impurity-delusion," the female sexual organ is meant.
"Whatever he might say," and so forth:
whatever speech a man, desiring to engage in sexual misconduct, might speak in the presence of a woman— however it may be, in whatever manner— a mendicant should not speak such words to a woman.
"In such and such a way" means by that or those respective modes.
"Agretyādi" and so forth. By the word "yoṣit," the female sex (mātṛgrāma) is designated.
A woman who would attend upon me—that is, perform service for me—from what [reason]? From privacy (rahaḥ).
The meaning is "in secret. She becomes foremost; she becomes the most excellent.
"Free from disease" means devoid of illness;
"renowned" means endowed with fame, possessed of glory.
And she becomes an attainer.
Of what? He says: of life-span and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of complexion, strength, happiness, and so forth.
One should not speak such words as these;
that is, one should not utter speech such as, "That woman is excellent," and so on.
Who is he? It is said:
Śrīghana (the Mass of Glory). Of what nature is he? It is said:
"One whose mind is scorched by the fire of passion":
passion itself is the fire; it is called the "fire of passion" because its nature is to burn.
One whose mind—that is, whose consciousness—is scorched or consumed by that is described in this way.
Before whom should one not speak? He says:
"In the presence of women, Śrīghana," and so forth;
that is, in front of women.
The meaning is: "of a man and of a eunuch."
To show that it is not permitted to act as a messenger for the purpose of uniting a woman and a man, he says:
"In the case of marriage and taking a wife," and so forth. Therein, "marriage" (*vivāha*) refers to the formal acceptance of a girl.
*Āvāha* means the taking in marriage of a girl who has not been enjoyed by another; *vivāha* means the giving away [of a daughter].

*Vivāhāvāhau* is the dual compound of *vivāha* and *āvāha*. Therefore, one should not perform the work of a messenger (*dautyakarma*) on account of those two—namely, for the sake of a wedding (*vivāha*) or for the sake of taking a wife (*āvāha*).
Who is he? It is said: the novice (śrāmaṇeraka). A novice himself is a novice.

Some, however, apply the suffix *kana* in the sense of contempt, as in "a contemptible novice" (*śrāmaṇeraka*). They must demonstrate the meaning of this contempt: in what way is this ascetic contemptible?
If it is argued that this is because he performs the work of a messenger, [we reply:
no, for this is not a prohibition stating "one should not do it";
rather, it concerns one who does not do it.
How does he incur reproach?
Therefore, this [term] *ka* should be understood as having its own specific meaning.

Not only should one not perform the office of a messenger for the purpose of marriage or bringing a bride, but—as the word "also" (*api*) indicates—one should not perform it even for the purpose of engaging in sexual intercourse at that very moment.
"I would cause her to be given," and so forth.
In this context, "faithful" (śrāddha) refers to one who possesses conviction regarding the truths of karma and its results, as well as the Jewels and so on.
To that faithful layman (upāsaka-dāraka), I would cause this faithful laywoman (upāsikā-dārikā) to be given.
Thus, it is not fitting for a renunciant to speak a sutra that flows with such worldly meaning.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of seed," and so forth:
for the purpose of producing offspring, one who observes the vow should not give away cows and the like;
nor should he ever request these very horses and other animals from others for the sake of seed.
"Equal toward these," and so forth:
a practitioner (yati) should not speak thus to a man who has many wives—namely, "Why do you stay with only one woman? Rather, you should dwell with all the women in turn."
In the *Sphuṭārthā*, the commentary on the *Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha*, this is the third precept regarding the abstention from sexual misconduct.
With reference to the training rule regarding abstention from false speech,
he says "Pratyekabuddha," and so forth.
In that context, one who is awakened for himself alone is a *pratyekabuddha*.
Those who have perfectly and non-erroneously awakened to all that is to be known are the *saṃbuddhas*.
Their disciples are "their disciples" (*tacchiṣyāḥ*).
Here, by the word "their" (*tat*), the *saṃbuddhas* themselves are intended.
It is not the Pratyekabuddhas, because [the word "and"] denotes what immediately follows it.
The analysis of the compound is: "Pratyekabuddhas, and Sambuddhas, and their disciples.
Whatever knowledge and vision they possess, that belongs to me.
"I possess [it]"—the meaning is that if a śrāmaṇera speaks falsely even when he does not actually possess it, he is to be expelled and should be held as no longer being a śrāmaṇera.
But what about one who speaks out of overweening pride (*abhimāna*)? Is he also to be expelled? No, he says.
"Except for pride.
The word "except" (*anyatra*) functions in the sense of exclusion.
This is because we observe the use of the word "except" in the sense of exclusion, as in: "All the warriors turned their backs, except for Bhīṣma and Droṇa."
*Abhimāna* (conceit) is that inflation of the mind which occurs when one thinks "I have attained" regarding a superior specific realization (*viśeṣādhigama*) that has not actually been attained.
Because of that conceit, one who professs knowledge and vision does not undergo a forfeiture of their vows, since they possess the notion that [the realization] has been attained.
Regarding what was said—that one who says "I possess knowledge and vision" is destroyed by falsehood—it is not understood therein what that knowledge is and what that vision is.
Therefore, with reference to the characteristic of knowledge and vision, he says:
"Knowledge is the perfect awakening to the truths," and so forth.
The truths are four, known as suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
In this context, the truth of suffering consists of the five aggregates of clinging;
the truth of origination is the craving that leads to renewed existence;
and the truth of cessation is the abandonment of this craving for renewed existence.
The truth of the path is this very Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention,
and right speech.
right action, right livelihood, and right effort;
Right mindfulness and right concentration.
In this context, awakening (*bodhana*) is awakening (*bodhi*), which means comprehension, understanding, and full knowledge, because its purpose is the knowledge of awakening.
The prefix *abhi* here functions in the sense of "facing toward" (*ābhimukhya*), while *sam* [in *samyak*] signifies "non-perversion" (*aviparītatva*).

Consequently, the meaning of the sentence arises as follows: that knowledge which is the awakening (*bodhi*) directed toward Nirvana regarding the Noble Truths of suffering and so forth, being correct and non-perverted, is called "knowledge."
"The five superknowledges are vision" means that "superknowledge" (abhijñā) refers to the knowledge of superknowledge (abhijñājñāna).
In that regard, there are five superknowledges.
The divine eye (*divyam cakṣus*), by which one sees forms that are extremely distant, subtle, or obstructed, as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit held in the palm of the hand;
the divine ear (*divyam śrotra*), by which sounds from far and near are heard—those of gods and humans, even down to an ant or a termite;

and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), by which one knows the mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of others—such as knowing a mind with passion (*sarāga-citta*) to be "with passion," and so forth.

The knowledge of recollecting former abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) is that by which one remembers the succession of births for oneself and others—such as "In such-and-such a place, I had this name, this clan," and so forth; the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*) is that by which one knows of oneself: "Birth is exhausted for me, the holy life has been lived, and there is no further state of being hereafter.
These five supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) are called the "vision" (*darśana*).
Demonstrating that the mention of "knowledge and vision" is for the purpose of illustration, he says:
"beginning with dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, and so forth.
Knowledge that has the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*) as its object is *dharma-jñāna*, by means of which one abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*).

That knowledge which arises as an introspective realization following after the mental continuums of others— realizing that those others who have previously abandoned the afflictions (*kleśa*), those who are currently abandoning them, or those who will abandon them in the future, have all attained, are attaining, or will attain precisely such knowledge— this is subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and so forth are included.

The knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), conventional knowledge (sāṃvṛtajñāna), the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), the knowledge of accomplishment (sādhyajñāna), the knowledge of signs (naimittikajñāna), and the seventh, known as the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna).
Thus is the verse concerning the seven knowledges.
If one accepts [the knowledge] of dharma and so forth, the previously mentioned [knowledge] is no longer appropriate; thus, there occurs the abandonment of the restraint.
"Ārya, mleccha," and so forth.

Here, by the word "ārya," persons born in the noble lands (āryadeśa) are intended, not those who have abandoned the afflictions (prahīṇakleśa); and by the word "mleccha," the Śavaras and others are meant.
Whatever is their speech, by means of that—having written it down in the form of a letter for one staying in another country, having transcribed it directly in writing—[one should send it].

"By means of a hand-gesture" refers to the arrangement of the fingers; "by means of a gesture of an elephant" refers to a mimetic performance. If a novice monk claims to possess knowledge, vision, and so forth, it should be understood that even such knowledge, vision, and so forth are false.
For one who informs others through letters and the like, there is no abandonment of the vow, because there is an absence of vocal utterance.
"At the foot of a tree," and so forth.

"I dwell alone and without a second at the foot of a tree, in an empty temple or house; I rejoice, and my mind is one-pointed and concentrated"—such matters concerning things beyond the senses must not be spoken by an ascetic.
He says this in order to prevent an over-extension of the principle.
Regarding the phrase "of the Buddha and others":
*varṇa* means quality (*guṇa*);
that [quality] must be proclaimed in many ways by the Tathāgata in the world, because it accomplishes the welfare of both oneself and others.
Thus, that Blessed One is endowed with the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the three foundations of mindfulness, and great compassion.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," the qualities of the Dharma and the Saṅgha are also implied;
however, one's own qualities must not be spoken of in any manner whatsoever.
"Kathañcana" means "in any way whatsoever.
When questioned, however, an ascetic may speak of another's existing virtues; even then, he should not do so in the presence of that virtuous person.

When he says, "That which he would speak in his presence," he does not [mean it] in that way; rather, intending to explain in detail the definition of false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*) whose intrinsic nature has not yet been understood, he sets forth the conventions of the noble and the non-noble, beginning with the words "seen" and so forth.
In this context, "seen" refers to what is experienced by visual consciousness, and "heard" refers to what is cognized by auditory consciousness.

Some maintain that what is cognized by the consciousnesses of the nose, tongue, and body, as well as by the mental consciousness, is "known" (*mata*). Others, however, say: that which is determined by the five sense-faculties is "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*); that which is received from another is "heard" (*śruta*).

That which is considered (*mata*) is what has been determined for oneself through reasoning; that which is known (*vijñāta*) is what has been delimited by the mind through a mode of experience personally realized within.
Regarding such [an object], when it is seen, one should say "it is seen," up to "it is known."
"Speaking erroneously" means being a speaker of falsehood. "Erroneousness" (*vaiparītya*) is the state of being contrary; the meaning is that it is by way of such ignoble conduct (*anāryavyavahāra*).
Furthermore, ignoble conducts include such things as claiming to have seen what was not seen.
"Speaking thus" means saying;
the meaning is that one would be a liar, a speaker of falsehood.
Furthermore, he asks: "By how many factors does one become a liar?
and states the verse beginning with "The object," and so forth:
"And there is an object," etc.
He possesses a false perception,
his mind is obscured,
and he has the notion that it is a lie.
And he utters speech.
He who possesses these five factors is "five-limbed" (*pañcāṅga*).
To the question "Who, then, is this?", he says:

"One who speaks untruth" (*anṛtavādika*) means one who possesses untruthful speech; that is to say, a liar. In this context, "it exists as an entity" means that it exists in accordance with how it is delimited, in terms of its meaning (*arthatas*), but not as a substantial reality (*dravyatas*).

For otherwise, if one knew that an object is non-existent and, having understood "it does not exist," were to say "it is not there," there would be no offense; moreover, one would possess a false perception—the meaning being that one has the perception, "I am speaking otherwise than what was determined. Furthermore, "the mind is set aside" means that it gives rise to speech that reveals something contrary to the object of knowledge as it was determined. (SŚ 56)
The meaning is that the mind becomes [so].
Even so, as to why it is stated separately— given that "being one who perceives a falsehood" is already included within this very [category]—
it is not the case that this is so.
The intention to deceive another is designated as "false speech" (*mṛṣāvāda*).

However, since that [intention] exists, the mind that gives rise to the speech—which conveys a meaning contrary to the object of knowledge as it has been correctly determined—is stated to be a distinct cause; thus, [the intention] is not included within that [speech].

Accordingly, in the Vinaya, it says: "Having set aside the perception (*saṃjñā*) and having set aside the mind (*citta*), one utters speech"; the meaning is that one becomes a speaker of false speech by having the intention to deceive another.

If it is asked, "What is the distinction between this and one who possesses a false perception? [the answer is: One who possesses a false perception explains a matter incorrectly, yet does not intend to deceive another;
thus, it is considered a lie (*mṛṣāvāda*), as in the case of saying, "The color of your face is radiant," and so forth.
This is not what is being said here.

One who possesses a false perception (*vitatha-saṃjñin*) does not necessarily possess the perception of falsehood (*mṛṣāvāda-saṃjñin*), whereas one who possesses the perception of falsehood necessarily possesses a false perception; thus, it is held that false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*) consists of these two factors alone.
"He should speak words" [is the phrase].
The meaning is that one utters speech.
This is what is being said: those words which possess four factors receive the designation of "false speech."
Intentional lying does not occur only through five factors;
rather, it occurs even through a single one. Demonstrating this, he says:
"four, three," and so forth.
From among those factors previously mentioned, a mendicant who speaks falsely while endowed with those factors that have been excluded from them should be known as a liar by other mendicants.
In this regard, one becomes a liar through four factors.
"Having a false perception," and so forth.
Because one grasps the object through the state of having a false perception, it is not mentioned separately.
"Established by three factors," and so forth.
Because the mind directed toward a false perception is already included within [the category of] lying; for it is said that "by means of two factors alone, one who perceives falsely," and so forth,
since that which is directed [toward a false object] is indeed included within lying itself.
There is conscious lying by means of a single factor, namely,
when one speaks words having set aside the mind [from its true intention].
Here too, the preceding factors are not mentioned separately because they are understood through implication.
Otherwise, it would have been stated that one becomes a liar by means of a single factor, up to five factors, for the purpose of establishing their number and sequence.
"By means of what is untrue," and so forth.
A practitioner (*yati*) should not accuse another practitioner (*yati*) face-to-face.
To the question "What kind of practitioner [should not do so]?", he says:

The term *dhvaṃsanacyāvanākūtaḥ* means one who has the intention (*ākūta*) of destroying or causing to fall away; *ākūta* here signifies intention. Thus, it means that one who intends to destroy or intends to incite [others] should not exert effort, nor should he cause [them] to arise; this is the meaning.
"Defamation" is the charging with faults; "destruction" is the expulsion from the state of one established in celibacy. To the question "By what means should one not incite [these]?", he says:
"By means of killing, taking what is not given, false speech, and so forth;
by that which is unreal," and so on.
Regarding the term "by that which is unreal," it means by that which does not exist.
"Without a cause" (*anidānena*) means "without a reason," since the word *anidāna* is a synonym for "lack of cause. Regarding "trifling," and so forth:

that offense is trifling, meaning very slight; it is designated as a *duṣkṛta*. That very [offense] is the sign or cause for the admonition; therefore, it is "by means of that trifling offense as the cause."
Alternatively, it means by even a slight degree, by even a minor misdeed, or by intention;
"by that very [intention]" means by the previously mentioned intention to destroy or cause downfall.
A novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*) should not revile others in their presence.
The meaning is "he should not speak of it.
Regarding the phrase "jāti-liṅga," etc.: *jāti* (birth), *anvaya* (lineage), and *kula* (family) have one and the same meaning.
*Liṅga* means a bodily mark;
*kriyā*, *karman*, "means of livelihood," and "mode of life" (*vṛtti*) are synonymous.
The word *vāda* is connected with each [of these terms].
The compound *jātivādaśca liṅgavādaśca* and so forth is a *dvandva*.

With these—each being inferior, middling, or superior—a practitioner (*vratī*) should never, at any time, reproach living beings (*pudgalān*) for the purpose of making them humble or for the purpose of rendering them speechless.
[This applies to] the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and so forth.
In this context, "affliction" (*upakleśa*) refers to dullness and so forth;
"disease" (*gada*) means illness;
and "reproach" (*ākrośa*) is censure on account of misconduct.
An offense (*āpatti*) is a transgression of the Blessed One’s command by means of body, speech, or mind.

A practitioner (*vratin*), through an affliction (*upakleśa*) or the like, should never speak with the aforementioned intention—that is, with the intent to make another practitioner dull-witted or speechless;
the meaning is that he should not say it at any time whatsoever.
And here, there is no distinction of inferior, middling, or superior, precisely because of the inferiority of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and so forth.
By these two verses, the fourfold deficiency of the person who raises the objection is stated: by the claim regarding [his] birth, the deficiency of his lineage is shown;
By the discourse on gender, the deficiency of the body is indicated; by the discourse on action, the deficiency of conduct is indicated;
and by transgressions, insults, and afflictions, the deficiency of qualities is stated.
The deficiency of virtues is proclaimed through offenses, insults, and afflictions;
likewise, [deficiencies in] lineage, gender, conduct, speech, family, body, and livelihood [are proclaimed].
Thus is the summary verse.
Showing that it is unbecoming for a renunciant and that backbiting is a transgression by nature, he says:
"It will lead to division," and so forth;
[meaning] this person will cause a rift with that person.
Thinking, "He will dwell together with me," an ascetic should not practice slander by speaking of [another's] caste and so forth.
In this regard, the abandonment of restraint (*saṃvara*) is explained by three *kārikās*, while the remaining verses describe the five limbs,
because the misdeeds (*aduṣkṛta*) have been cited therein.
If one causes ignorant persons to hear of the non-existence of the attainment of dhyāna and so forth,
or else, how could the restraint not be abandoned due to an informative act of ignorance?
Thus ends the riddle.
In the *Sphuṭārthā*, the commentary on the *Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha*, this is the fourth precept: abstaining from false speech.
Having reached the appropriate occasion, he speaks with reference to the training precept regarding the abstinence from drinking fermented liquor,
distilled spirits, and intoxicants, beginning with the words "intoxicant" and so forth.

This is because the drinking of fermented liquor, distilled spirits, and intoxicants is the locus and foundation of negligence— that is, the lack of heedfulness toward wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*).
For that reason, yogis should neither give that *surā*, *maireya*, or *madya* to another, nor drink it themselves.
To explain why—namely, for the purpose of removing ignorance, doubt, and error in those who are ignorant, doubtful, or mistaken—he provides an illustration:
"like dog urine."
Just as dog urine is neither given to another nor drunk by oneself, in the same way, a *śrāmaṇera* must not give *surā*, *maireya*, or *madya* to another, nor should he drink it himself.
There is also a reading *svamūtravat*; its explanation there is "like one's own urine. In that context, *sura* refers to liquor (*āsava*).
That which is accumulated by means of food and its various transformations should be understood as being threefold. To explain how this is so, he says:
"With bark and jaggery," and so forth:
one type of *surā* is prepared from bark combined with jaggery,
while another is made from honey alone.
Flour is *apūpa*, yeast is *kiṇva* (the seed of *surā*),
and water is *jala*.
Since some liquor is also produced by these [plants], these too should be understood as liquors.
"Maireya," and so forth;
*dhātrī* is the fruit of the *āmalaka* tree,
and *ambu* is water.
*Dhātakī* is simply a species of flower well-known in the world.
That distinct flavor (*rasāntara*) which is prepared and produced by means of jaggery, *dhātrī*, water, and *dhātakī* is called *maireya*.

Since this liquor made from *surā* and *maireya* is intoxicating, it is not permissible for ascetics (*yatayaḥ*) or novices (*śrāmaṇerāḥ*) to drink even as much as a drop on the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass.
It is not obtained;
it is not only unfit to be drunk like water and so forth, but by using the word "even" (api), he indicates that it is unfit even [to be touched] with the tip of a blade of kusha grass.
Showing that no other intoxicating substance besides *surā* and *maireya* is permitted for consumption, he says:
"kodravānna," and so forth.
An ascetic (*yati*) should not eat *kodrava* grain.
And he should not sleep on the straw of that *kodrava* grain;
"he would become intoxicated," and so forth.
Furthermore, whatever else— other than *surā* and *maireya*— has the color, smell, and taste of intoxicants, and which, when drunk, causes intoxication or generates a state of intoxication,
that too must not be drunk;
for one who drinks it, demerit arises.
For this very reason, having recognized that betel nuts and similar items are intoxicants, they should not be consumed.
If a novice monk should drink *surā*, *maireya*, or *madya* liquor,
or eat *kodrava* grain, how could there not be a transgression?
Thus ends the riddle.
In the *Sphuṭārthā*, the commentary on the *Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha*, the fifth chapter, titled "The Training Rule Concerning Abstinence from Drinking Surā, Maireya, and Madya," is completed.
The training precept characterized by abstaining from drinking fermented liquors, spirits, and intoxicants has been explained.
Now, having found the opportunity, he speaks of the training precept characterized by abstaining from high and grand beds, beginning with:
"The ascetic should sit upon a bed," and so forth.
In this context, because he has conquered the afflictions (*kleśa*), the Blessed One is the Victor (*jina*).
A bed or seat whose legs are of that measure—namely eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*)—of his is called a "bed or seat with legs of eight fingers of the Victor" (*jināṣṭāṅgulapādaka*).
Furthermore, this measurement of eight fingers of the Victor is three times the measurement of eight fingers of an ordinary person.
Thus, there are twenty-four finger-breadths;
by that, it is designated as the measure of a "hand" (*hasta*).
A monk (*yati*) or a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) should sit—that is, take a seat—upon a bed or a bench whose legs are of the measure of a hand according to the standard human measurement.
Is it together with the thorn? He says, "No.
What then? It is without the thorn;
the meaning is, having abandoned the thorn.
Therefore, whoever sits upon a couch or a seat that exceeds the prescribed measure incurs an offense of wrongdoing (*duṣkṛta*);
however, this does not apply to those made of gold or silver.
However, it is not permitted to sit upon a couch or a seat made of gold or silver, even if they are only eight finger-breadths in size.
Now, for what purpose is this stated— "not on that which is made of gold or silver"—
when it will later be said that one may use the body, hands, feet, and so forth, as well as garments, parasols, and the like?
And where the touch of clothing and so forth is prohibited, there enjoyment is all the more impossible;
this is true.

However, someone might have this doubt: "There is no fault for one sitting on a bed or seat made of gold or silver belonging to the Saṃgha, because the prohibition regarding touch applies only to what belongs to an individual (pudgala). To address this, the following is stated;
some explain the resolution as follows:
This is incorrect, because there is no distinction made; the touching of gold and silver belonging both to the Saṅgha and to an individual is equally prohibited.
Therefore, an effort must be made for the sake of avoidance.
Even there, it is shown that one is not permitted to sit upon a couch or a seat measuring eight finger-breadths of a *jina* without a covering;

thus he says, "one should give [a covering] on a bed belonging to the Saṃgha," and so forth. That which belongs to the Saṃgha is "belonging to the Saṃgha" (*sāṃghika*), referring to the bedding and seating.
In that regard, the ascetic should provide a seat-covering (pratyāstaraṇa).
And by "seat-covering," what is intended is not grass, leaves, or the like, but rather a *viṣṭara* (matted seat), as he says.
Regarding the passage beginning with "vastra" and so forth:
for fine cloth, a three-layered spread is desired; for thick cloth, a two-layered one; and for woolen blankets, a single-layered one is intended—meaning it is what is approved.
"Successively" means according to order;
the meaning is that one should understand the distinction of three, two, or one layer for the underlaying cloth.
He explains how one should deal with surplus communal bedding and seats that exceed the standard measure, stating:
"having placed its feet in the pits," and so forth.
By the word "its" (tat), the communal bedding and seat is referred to.
"Those feet" refers to the feet of the bedding and seating belonging to the Saṃgha.
Of what kind? Excessive in measure;
that is to say, exceeding the measure of eight finger-breadths of a Jina.
"Having deposited," that is, having thrown; where? He says: "into pits."
Or alternatively, having cast it into hollow receptacles;
why indeed would one observing the vows make use of bedding and seating belonging to the Saṅgha?
"Bedding and seating" is what will be explained hereafter.
"Or having fixed [the feet] upon stakes":

alternatively, having fixed and bound the feet—which are of a length exceeding those [stakes]—upon four stakes, it is not known what should be done, because the connection between the action and its agent has not been completed.
Therefore, he says "in this way," and so forth.
In the sequence just described, one should utilize the bedding and seating belonging to the Saṅgha.
For the purpose of protecting sugarcane, barley, wheat, and so forth, a bed with long legs is constructed; [one should not use such a bed].
In that regard, a traveling ascetic may sleep;
by the word "etcetera," it should be understood that the beds and seats of householders are included.
Even there, on the beds and seats of householders, the ascetic must not let his feet hang down, lest it cause people to harbor ill-will.
Demonstrating that, having authorized the going forth, the communal monastery (*saṃghika-vihāra*) should be assigned according to seniority (*yathāvṛddhikayā*), he says:
"If it is small," and so forth.
If there are many novices (*śrāmaṇera*) but few monasteries, then each monastery should be assigned to twelve novices.
Now, if there are many renunciants even in this way, then, as a last resort when there is no other way, one handful (nirmuṣṭaka) must be given to each novice (śrāmaṇera);
however, if they are numerous, it is the reverse.
How is it by way of reversal?
If there are many monasteries and few ascetics, then many monasteries should be assigned even to a single novice.
In this context, by the word "vihāra," only a dwelling place (layana) is meant, based on the derivation that they dwell (*viharanti*) therein.
Regarding the passage beginning with "If it is small," etc.:
if the bedding and seats are few while the ascetics are many, then in that case, he who is the most senior should sleep on the couch.
But he who is a junior (navaka) should sleep on a mat.
If, even so, this is not possible for everyone,
then the senior (vṛddha) should sleep at the foot of a tree.

The bedding and seating belonging to the Saṃgha should be assigned according to seniority, starting with the newest monk and ending with the most senior, thinking, "This one is for the one who stays in the open air.
But is this to be done at all times? He says:
"It should not be set aside during the rains," and so forth.
During the period between the rains retreats, a mendicant must not cause another fellow-practitioner to be ordained according to seniority;
whoever does so incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Now, he explains for what purpose the bedding and seating are intended,
beginning with the words "refinement" (saṃskāra) and so forth.
Refinement is the act of cutting the knots [of the afflictions] and so on.
In this context, "use" refers to abiding in one's own person;
"preservation" refers to guarding it.
Thus, he shows that the bedding and seating belonging to the Saṅgha is intended for this purpose, and not out of mere indulgence.
Furthermore, must all dwellings be designated? No, he says.
What then? "Inferior, middling," and so forth.
If there are many dwellings but the monks who observe the vows are few, then three dwellings should be set aside for the residence of visiting monks. He explains what kind they should be:
Whether it be inferior, middling, or superior;
if guests arrive, then one should assign it to the elders among the guests according to their seniority, starting from the youngest.
Among those three shelters, the best shelter should be assigned to an elderly guest-monk; the middle one to one who is younger than him; and the inferior one to all those who are the most junior.
But for what reason did the Blessed One prohibit high beds and grand couches?
He says: "A bed or seat that is excessively high," and so forth.
Because an excessively high bed or seat causes intoxication in a practitioner or a novice monk.
Because it causes restlessness and is a cause and condition for worldly attachment, for that reason the Blessed One prohibited high beds and large couches.
A high bed and a luxurious bed are so called because their dimensions exceed the eight-finger-width measure of a Jina, and because they are made of gold and silver respectively.
In the *Sphuṭārthā*, the commentary on the *Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha*, this is the sixth training rule, titled "Abstaining from High and Luxurious Beds."
With reference to the training rule concerning dancing, singing, instrumental music, [the sight of spectacles, and sensual pleasures], he says:
"with the flinging of arms," and so forth.
Dancing is defined as that which is performed by moving and tossing both arms about.
The Blessed One has declared that this dancing is madness;
and that which is sung in a loud voice is, for the Noble Ones—who have uprooted all roots of unwholesomeness and are skilled in rending the veil of ignorance—merely weeping and wailing.
For this reason, because the Blessed One spoke thus, an ascetic should not play musical instruments such as the lute, the flute, or the drum.

A renunciant should not go to a place of amusement—such as a festival or the like—where men and women, having gone there, become free from sorrow; he should not go to such a place of amusement that is "free from sorrow.
However, if a novice monk, being joyful, dances, sings, or plays musical instruments, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense for him.
In the *Sphuṭārthā*, the commentary on the *Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha*, this is the seventh training rule, titled "Abstaining from Dancing, Singing, Music, and [Visoka’s] Views."
With reference to the precept of abstaining from perfumes, garlands, and ointments,
it says "sandalwood," and so forth:
an ascetic (*yati*) may wear fragrances such as sandalwood.
He explains what kind of ascetic [is meant]:
one for whom disease has arisen is "afflicted" (vyādhita), meaning one who is ill.
He asks, "By whose word should one uphold [this]? He replies, "By that of the physician and others," meaning, "from the instruction of a doctor."
He asks, "By what procedure? and replies with the words beginning "having given," and so forth:
first, having offered sandalwood and other fragrances to the Sage, the Blessed Buddha, one should afterwards wear them oneself.
A self-composed ascetic, however, should never at any time wear fragrances such as sandalwood.
"He should not stand," and so forth.
In an open space, even if he is ill, a mendicant whose body is anointed with sandalwood and other unguents should not remain standing.
If he wishes to go outside, [he should do so].
Then, having washed [the hands], one should go outside;
by this very procedure, one should wear a garland of flowers (*kusumasraja*).
"Flower" (*kusuma*) means *puṣpa*.
"Srak" means "mālā";
thus, "kusumasraj" means a garland of flowers, that is to say, a flower wreath.
What should one wear?
According to this very rule:
first, one should offer it to the Buddha, and afterwards, one may wear it oneself.
To explain what kind of sick person should wear garlands and wreaths, he says:
"With eye-pain," and so forth.
A practitioner who is habitually afflicted by eye-pain, headache, and possession by the *pūtana* demon is described in that way.
One should encircle his head with a garland of flowers,
but one should not let a girdle hang from the flower garland.
Regarding the passage beginning with "haritāla" and so forth:

for the sake of color—that is, for the purpose of producing a physical form—a practitioner (yati) should not apply substances such as yellow orpiment or fragrant oil to his face or other parts of the body.
But for what reason did the Blessed One prohibit dancing and so forth? He says:
"Because it is unbecoming for an ascetic," and so on.
Since the sight of dancing, singing, instrumental music, and theatrical performances, as well as the wearing of perfumes, garlands, and ointments, is unbecoming for an ascetic and produces passion.
Because it causes agitation among people, is a cause for anger, and leads to lack of mindfulness, it has been censured and condemned by the Jinas, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
In this context, he prohibits other things as well with the words "not in a mirror" and so forth:
one should not look at one's face in a mirror, in an oil vessel, or in a water vessel.
Except for one who is afflicted or weakened by a disease such as a headache— characterized by pain in the head or the distress of piercing headaches— he should not look at another person.
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "for the sake of adornment," an ascetic should not anoint his face with oil for the purpose of beautification, nor even with water.
"Head-disease," and so forth:
"head-disease" refers to a sickness or affliction in the head;
he is described as such whose mouth—that is, his face—is cracked.
"Therefore, by nothing else" means [by no other substance].
"Not saffron," and so forth:
an ascetic (yati) should not adorn his face—that is, his mouth—with powders of sandalwood, saffron, and the like.

However, for the sake of healing a boil, an ointment made from a cluster of sesame seeds and so forth is desired— that is, it is intended— as a remedy. But for that ascetic who, due to negligence or similar reasons, does not carry out the prescribed rule,
there is an offense of wrongdoing (duṣkṛta).
In the *Sphuṭārthā*, the commentary on the *Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha*, this is the eighth training rule, titled "Abstaining from Perfumes, Garlands, and Ointments."
Demonstrating the reason for the prohibition against eating at improper times, he says:
"Of the night," and so forth.
Apart from the night, during the day, the Blessed One, while performing his meal-related activities, correctly perceived that he was free from illness.
"Bhikṣus," he said to the disciples; "What is it? [He replied: "Your task is exactly as before."
"Since I became free from illness when eating at times other than night,
therefore you too should eat during the day and not at night.
By this verse, the reason for the establishment of the training rule regarding the abstention from eating at improper times is explained.
Furthermore, in order to demonstrate that cause, he says:
"Feces, urine," and so forth.
For those wandering for alms at night, there is the danger of falling into pits of filth or pits of urine.
They encountered horse-thieves, cow-thieves, and even snakes and serpents.
Even so, people criticized them, saying, "These ascetics wander for alms in our houses at night merely for the sake of filling their bellies and stomachs.
Despite being thus criticized by the people, those ascetics began to wander for alms during the day—at dawn and in the evening as well.
To show that even there they were despised by the people,
he says the verse beginning with "In the evening and in the morning," and so forth:
"These monks wander and roam about in the evenings and in the mornings at the times of assembly, in the squares, crossroads, temples, and houses, and they eat while performing acts of disrespect."
It was disregarded by people;
therefore, for that reason, he asks "why?
and says, "The Sugata said," and so forth.
He is called *sugata* because he has gone (*gata*) to what is praiseworthy (*praśasta*), or to the state of non-return (*apunarāvṛtti*), or to the state of being without remainder (*niḥśeṣa*),
respectively like one who is well-formed (*surūpa*), like one whose debt is fully paid (*sunṛṣṭarṇa*), and like a jar that is completely full (*supūrṇaghaṭa*).
He said, "I am a practitioner" (*bratīti sma*).
What is this?
One should eat at the proper time.
At what kind of time? To this he says:
"Uditāditya," and so forth.
That midday during which the sun has risen even by the measure of a hair's breadth—that is, has not yet passed—is referred to as "udita-āditya"; [the meal is to be taken] at that time.
Furthermore, he explains what kind of food should be eaten at the time when the sun has risen:
"Barley meal, boiled rice," and so forth.
There are five types of food that are "timely" (*kālika*), namely: barley meal (*saktu*), boiled rice (*bhakta*), sour gruel (*kulmāṣa*), fish, and meat.
He says [the following] because these five foods may sometimes be mixed with those that are "seven-day" (*saptāhika*) and so on.
"Life-long," and so forth.
That which is excluded by life-long [medicines] such as long pepper (*pippalī*) and the like, as well as by oils and drinks, is "timely" (*kālika*).
But is it only these five kinds of food that are "timely," or is there something else as well?
He says "and other things as well," namely "whatever is eaten with the teeth.
By this, a substance that is hard and crisp is designated.
By the phrase "or what is swallowed through the throat," even that which is drunk through the nose is understood to be ingested by means of the throat;
thus, its prohibition is also established.
Otherwise, drinking milk at an improper time would not constitute an offense.
By the term *kukṣiviṣṭa*, the object denoted by both words is expressed.

It is called *kukṣiviṣṭambhakṛt* because it acts as a support for and fills the belly. All of this [should be eaten] at that time, meaning when the sun has risen and before midday; one should eat the sacrificial food (*yati-bhakṣayet*).
Showing what may be obtained for eating at the improper time (*vikāla*), he says:
"free from barley-meal and other kinds of meat," and so forth.
