It is abandoned by impurities such as flour and boiled grain;
of what nature is it? It is stainless, meaning free from dust, mud, and the like. When the god rains, whatever stone falls [is it].
He should eat—that is, consume—that hailstone;
"thirst" is the desire to drink, the longing for a beverage;
being afflicted by that, the ascetic should drink snow—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Furthermore, having raised the question of how "fit water" (kalpikodaka) is to be accepted, he says "the taking of fit water," etc., in order to provide the occasion for its discussion.
"The taking of fit water" (kalpavārigraha) means the acceptance of water that is permissible; [the phrase refers to] in that regard.
The taking of permissible water means as much as is necessary;
that is to say,
for as long as it takes to wash both hands until they become covered with blood.
For that duration of time, those two should not be washed;
nor should one take even a drop of permissible water for washing the fingers.
"Illusion," and so forth.
A practitioner endowed with deceit and guile should not perform the washing of those two; if a mendicant is naturally smooth-skinned,
then the two hands of that smooth-skinned practitioner will make a sound.
Then, the two [elements] are to be known as pure.
Furthermore, he says "you will not give," etc., to address the question of whether even one who is ill should not eat at an improper time;
*kṣud* means hunger.

Even by the word "thirst," the meaning commonly understood in the world— namely, the desire for drink— is expressed. If some ascetic, having been rebuked, were to say, "I shall die, tormented by those two [hunger and thirst], if you do not give me food at the improper time," [then one should respond as follows].
Then that ascetic should be thrown into a full pit of caustic matter until only his neck remains visible.
If, even so, one is unable to pass the time [until the end of the day], [the procedure continues].
To the question "What should be done then?", he says:
"Washed eight times in water," and so forth.

The meaning is that one should instruct the placing—in a vessel free from meat, such as a copper bowl or otherwise—of that grain which has been washed eight times in water and tied with a ritual cloth (*kalpika-vastu*). He should give it.
However, if that grain is clearly split or has become cracked, it is not permitted for one who is ill to drink it.
In this context, he also prohibits other things by way of an incidental discussion,
beginning with "aroused by greed" and so forth.

Whatever bodily or vocal action is aroused by greed, which is an unwholesome root, and whatever dwelling, robes, or food are acquired through that [action], one should avoid them as if they were poisoned food.
"Regarding 'madya' and so forth:
the selling of intoxicants,
the selling of weapons,"
One who observes the vow should not personally engage in the sale of poison, the sale of living beings, or the sale of lac.
Nor should one cause others to do so, nor should one make a livelihood by means of that liquor and such;
[this applies to] honoring and so forth.
The "senses" (akṣāṇi) are said to be the faculties, such as the eye and so forth;
the restraint or control over them for the sake of gain and honor is considered hypocrisy (kuhanā).
Furthermore, that flattery and pleasant speech which is employed for the sake of obtaining gains such as clothing, food, drink, and so forth, is considered "enticement" (*lāpanā*).
This refers to "extortion" (*naiṣpeṣikatva*) and the like.

To disparage others for the sake of obtaining food, drink, and so forth is called *naiṣpeṣikatva* (coercion). However, to praise or extol the virtues of another's bowl or other requisites for the sake of gain— thinking, "One should give this great bowl and so forth"— is called *naimittikatva* (hinting),
as expressed in the passage beginning with "one should seek through gain."
The pursuit of further gain through the gain already obtained is called "the desire for gain" (*lipsā*); by its meaning, *lipsā* is the wish to acquire more.
A practitioner should avoid those forms of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*) that are produced by such means as hypocrisy (*kuhana*), flattery (*lapanā*), and coercion (*naiṣpeṣikatā*).
What does he say?
He means "like excrement," that is, like impurity.
"Play" and so forth.
Depriving others [of their possessions], harming others, playfulness and curiosity, and constant arrogance of body and speech at all times.
Just as a practitioner of vows would avoid a snake smeared with excrement, like a serpent covered in impurity;
[this refers to] "the marketplace," and so forth.
*Vipaṇi* refers to a marketplace,
which is commonly known among the common people as a *ghaṭṭa*;
it is called *tara* because one crosses (*taranti*) upon it.
At the Kṣepaṇa-tīrtha, at a thicket, at a branch, and in such places—whether concealed or exposed—on a patch of ground, it will be stated: "Why should one remain there? Not as a novice (cellaka)."
Even though she is one who has gone forth as a wicked renunciant and is of immoral conduct, she remains within her vow.
He said:
"She is a renunciant in the form of a courtesan, making a living thereby."
The Guru says: A maiden living in a place remains unmarried.
What are these places? The house of a gambler, a prison, and any other place of confinement is declared to be an improper domain and an unsuitable sphere.
Therefore, one should not stay there.
In the *Sphuṭārthā*, the commentary on the *Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha*, this concludes the ninth training rule, titled "Abstaining from Eating at Improper Times."
With reference to the tenth precept,
he says "with the body," and so forth:
with his entire body— with both hands, both feet, clothing, and such items as a parasol— the one observing the vow [should avoid] silver, that is, *rūpya*.
One should not touch gold, that is, refined metal;
as to what it is like, he says:
it is like blazing fire.
"Like a blazing fire"—
by this, the tenth precept is stated.
Now, by means of this incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*), he includes other forms of conduct as well, beginning with "campū-kalaha" and so forth.
In that context, *campū* refers to laughter,
and *kalaha* refers to both physical quarreling and verbal quarreling.
"Chewing the tooth-stick" (*dantakāṣṭhādana*) means eating the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭhabhakṣaṇa*).
The rest is easy to understand.
"The quarrel with the *campū*" and so forth is a *dvandva* compound.

He is so described because he is an ascetic (*yati*) who has grown old in the presence of his preceptor (*vṛddhāntika*), performing such acts as chewing betel-nut (*campū*), quarreling, and brushing his teeth.
He is called "thus" because he is occupied with, or finds no opportunity for, bathing, drinking, eating, and reciting hymns (*snānapānāśanastotra*).
Furthermore, there is a compound analysis [of the term *snātaka*] as "one occupied with bathing and so forth," "one who is naked," and "one who wears a single garment.
It will be stated: "Why is that previously mentioned ascetic not to be saluted by an ascetic?
[The verse begins with] "the work of clay," and so forth.
He who is occupied with work involving clay and has not yet found the opportunity; he who desires to quickly and swiftly build a monastery of two or three stories; he who moves rapidly and speedily;
and he who bakes a bowl.

Or, if he is preoccupied with the work of robes, that ascetic at the end of the row of elders—rising from a monastery of two or three stories, or even while preparing his bowl—is not to be saluted; for it will be said: "Is one ascetic not to be saluted by another ascetic?
[The text continues with] "powder," and so forth.
He who is attached to the preparation of powders, to the making of garments, and to the cleaning of robes, bowls, and so forth;
or he who anoints his eyes or inhales smoke,
or writes a book.
He who causes [the text] to be recited is also not to be saluted;
such as the *viṭ*, *prastrāva*, and so forth.
If a novice monk goes to a latrine or a urinal,
or designates it for another,
or stays in darkness or deep gloom;
Whether he is wearing an inner garment (*antarvāsa*) or putting on an upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*),

that ascetic who stands at the end of the seniority row is not to be saluted by a junior as long as he is going toward the latrine or while putting on his upper robe; by this [rule], it is shown in what state an ascetic standing at the end of the seniority row remains when he is addressed by a junior.
It should not be saluted;
that state has been described.
Now, however, in order to demonstrate the kind of state in which a novice ascetic must not speak, he says:
"With [the head] covered," and so forth.
By what ascetic (yati) should one be saluted? It will be stated [later]: by one whose head is covered—meaning an ascetic whose head is veiled—or by one who is completely enveloped.
"Sopānatka" refers to one whose feet are together with sandals;
the meaning is: by one who has put on sandals.
"Knee and knee" means "two knees";
one should not strike a blister upon the shank of those two knees with a blunt object.
To what is this comparable? He says:
As with a ram:
"ram" (avi) refers to a male sheep;
as when one is struck on the two knees or the shanks by means of a ram (*meṇḍaka*).
In the same way, a monk should not prostrate at the shank of a senior monk; that is the extent of the rule. However, the Venerable Dharmāvalokitamitra says:
"One should not prostrate while wearing shoes."
To the question "What is it like?", he says:
"As by the sun. "Sun" (ravi) refers to the Āditya.

Just as that sun [is not to be saluted] when mounted upon shoes, so too a renunciant who is mounted upon shoes should not be saluted; thus he speaks, making his meaning understood through the elision of the letter *a* (in the word *na-vandanīya*). Should this be accepted as the venerable teacher’s view? It should not be accepted.
What then? It must be investigated, because the example of the ram (*meḍhaka*) was given in the Vinaya.
Showing the procedure, he says:
"In the state of equipoise," and so forth.
Having grasped the pair of feet of the ascetic seated in equipoise with both hands like a crab, he should pay homage with his head.
When a mendicant is seated in the assembly hall and is afflicted by a foot ailment, there is no fault in his being saluted even without the use of the *karkaṭagrāhikā* (the crab-grip).
If some guest should come and salute one who is seated in the assembly hall, he should then say: "Venerable sir," (SŚ 76)
How many years have you been [ordained],
which school do you belong to, and how many divisions are there in that school?
"What is this 'occasional' [attainment] of yours? and so forth.
If he is an Ārya-Mahāsāṃghika, then he should say, "I am an Ārya-Mahāsāṃghika."
If there are divisions of that [school],
they are the Mūlasāṃghikas, who have six branches: the Bhādrāyaṇas, the Haimavatas, and those residing on two mountains, whose purposes are accomplished through their doctrines.
The long [retreat], the winter, the summer, the rainy, and likewise the subsequent one—
these five collective [retreats] should be understood by a novice monk (śrāmaṇera).
In this manner, other [matters] as well should be avoided.
In that regard, the junior one should pay homage,
and the senior one should say, "May you be free from illness."
Now, what is the meaning of "health"?
Just as wind, bile, phlegm, and so forth, when provoked, are called "diseases" (roga) in the sense that they cause affliction,
likewise the afflictions (kleśa), such as passion and the rest, are denoted by the word "disease" in the sense that they cause suffering.
Disease is the absence of health; the state of being free from disease is health.
May you possess the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Thus it has been said:
"For passion and the like cause far greater suffering than the provoked humors such as wind do for the entire multitude of beings."
Therefore, those Buddhas who are supremely desirous of peace for others utter these words to those who bow before them: "May there be health."
Another says:
That which is liberated from old age, death, sorrow, and fear;
that which is devoid of the moon, fire, sun, and water.
That which is the eternal, unsurpassed, and infallible state...

"Since all the monks who desire training have engaged in eating at improper times and so forth, why should we not do the same?"—this is the "justification by residence. "In this monastery, the monks engage in physical contact with one another; why should we not do the same?"—this is the "justification by region.
"In that region, there are monks who act as usurers; why should we not also lend money at interest?"—this is the "justification by region."
The Elder’s Rule: "Even such-and-such an elder eats at the time of the junction;
why should we not eat?"
In order to show that this is a different practice extracted from the *Bhikṣu-vinaya* and not something else composed according to his own fancy, he says:
"The Vinaya. It is called *vinaya* because by means of it, the afflictions (*kleśa*) are disciplined (*vinayante*).
This has been extracted from the summary of the Bhikṣu-vinaya by one who has attained the Prātimokṣa vows.

As for the remainder, which is taught extensively in the Bhikṣu-vinaya— namely, how one should conduct oneself regarding food, clothing, and so forth— that must be heard from the presence of the upādhyāya, the ācārya, and other seniors by the ascetic.
"One should be possessed of reverence by means of the two hundred [verses]," and so forth.

Having condensed this *Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha* spoken in the interim, by whatever merit (*sukṛta*) or wholesome deed (*kuśalakṛta*) has been performed, may people—the world—attain and obtain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), which is nirvāṇa; it is by means of this [that one prays].
He dedicates by means of a verse.
Thus, having composed this commentary, Jayarakṣita,
which steals away the thieves that plunder the scriptures of all people—
May all people, by virtue of the vast merit that I have acquired, become Buddhas.
By whatever merit has been gained from composing this commentary on the *Suśrīghanācārasusaṃgraha*,
may all people, through that auspiciousness, swiftly become Jinas, possessing the glory of the arising of renowned virtues.
